lectures.title: Disorders of the External and Middle Ear

fields.name: Eustachian tube dysfunction
fields.definition: Not covered in the lecture
fields.etiology: Most commonly edema of the tissue lining the tube secondary to upper respiratory infection or allergy; often transient (days to weeks)
fields.pathology: Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx, is closed except during swallowing or yawning, and passes air to equalize pressure (can also let fluid into the middle ear); edema of its lining blocks it
fields.clinical: Sensation of ear fullness; mild-moderate hearing impairment; crackling/popping with yawning or swallowing (indicates partial blockage of the tube)
fields.diagnosis: Physical exam: retraction of the tympanic membrane; decreased mobility with insufflation
fields.treatment: Systemic or intranasal decongestants; intranasal corticosteroids; forced exhalation against resistance (caution with active nasal discharge: may force fluid into the middle ear and trigger acute otitis media); education: avoid air travel or other altitude/pressure changes until symptoms resolve

fields.name: Acute otitis media (AOM); suppurative otitis media (discharge into the external canal through a tympanic membrane perforation); recurrent AOM
fields.definition: Rapid-onset inflammation of the middle ear; recurrent AOM = 3 or more episodes in 6 months or >4 episodes in 12 months, with complete resolution between episodes
fields.etiology: Most often follows upper respiratory illness; eustachian tube dysfunction (inflammation from respiratory illness or allergies; obstruction by adenoid hypertrophy or other masses); most common bacteria Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis
fields.epidemiology: Otitis media is most common in the pediatric population, peak incidence around 2 years of age; adults are 3-15% of acute otitis media diagnoses
fields.pathology: Eustachian tube dysfunction leads to middle ear inflammation with purulent effusion; if the tympanic membrane perforates, discharge drains into the external canal (suppurative otitis media)
fields.clinical: Otalgia; fever; hearing loss; complications: tympanic membrane perforation, mastoiditis (infection spreads to the mastoid air cells), labyrinthitis (infection spreads to the labyrinth), meningitis/encephalitis (rare)
fields.diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis; exam (varies with degree of infection): erythematous and/or bulging tympanic membrane, purulent effusion often visible, decreased mobility on pneumatic otoscopy, possible cervical lymphadenopathy; tympanometry optional (quantitative tympanic membrane mobility)
fields.treatment: Most episodes resolve spontaneously; antibiotics for bacterial involvement (e.g., amoxicillin); analgesics and antipyretics for otalgia and fever; consider tympanostomy tubes for refractory/recurrent episodes or complications (ENT (ear, nose, and throat specialist))

fields.name: Otitis media with effusion (OME); serous otitis media (serous effusion)
fields.definition: Inflammation of the middle ear space with an effusion present
fields.etiology: Eustachian tube dysfunction trapping fluid in the middle ear space; effusion often present after bacterial acute otitis media resolves
fields.epidemiology: Otitis media overall is most common in the pediatric population, peak incidence around 2 years of age (stated for otitis media as a group)
fields.pathology: Fluid effusion trapped in the middle ear by eustachian tube dysfunction; may be serous (serous otitis media)
fields.clinical: Often asymptomatic (may be an incidental otoscopy finding); hearing loss; sensation of ear fullness; complications: temporary conductive hearing loss (speech/language delay in children), acquired cholesteatoma
fields.diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis; exam: dull tympanic membrane, air/fluid level often visible, decreased mobility on pneumatic otoscopy, possible cervical lymphadenopathy with recent respiratory illness or resolved acute otitis media; tympanometry optional
fields.treatment: Most episodes resolve spontaneously; management depends on duration of fluid, degree of hearing loss, and effect on speech/language development; tympanostomy tubes (ENT (ear, nose, and throat specialist)); consider adenoidectomy if adenoid hypertrophy obstructs the eustachian tubes (ENT)

fields.name: Chronic otitis media (COM); subtypes: benign COM, COM with effusion (chronic serous otitis media), chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM)
fields.definition: Recurrent infections with a non-healing perforation of the tympanic membrane
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Otitis media overall is most common in the pediatric population, peak incidence around 2 years of age (stated for otitis media as a group)
fields.pathology: Non-healing tympanic membrane perforation; benign COM = dry perforation with no active infection; COM with effusion = continuous serous drainage through the perforation; CSOM = persistent purulent drainage through the perforation
fields.clinical: Recurrent infections; serous or purulent drainage through the perforation depending on subtype (dry in benign COM)
fields.diagnosis: Duration required for diagnosis is controversial (varies from weeks to months)
fields.treatment: Refer to ENT (ear, nose, and throat specialist)

fields.name: Barotrauma
fields.definition: Not covered in the lecture
fields.etiology: Inability to equalize pressure in the middle ear; seen during air travel, rapid altitude changes, SCUBA (self-contained underwater breathing apparatus) diving
fields.risk_factors: Pressure changes while respiratory illness or allergy exacerbation is present; frequent flying (recurrent episodes)
fields.pathology: Can rupture the tympanic membrane or cause middle ear hemorrhage; severe cases involve the inner ear with rupture of the round or oval window
fields.clinical: Otalgia; conductive hearing loss; inner ear complications: tinnitus, sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo, nausea and vomiting
fields.diagnosis: Exam: decreased tympanic membrane (TM) mobility on insufflation; hemotympanum (visible blood in the middle ear) if hemorrhage; visible perforation if present
fields.treatment: Equalize by swallowing, yawning, exhaling through the nose against resistance; oral/intranasal decongestants; myringotomy gives instant relief (reserved for severe otalgia and hearing loss with intact membranes, ENT (ear, nose, and throat specialist)); tympanostomy tubes for recurrent episodes in frequent flyers (ENT); prevention: avoid pressure changes when ill, or equalize and take decongestants beforehand

fields.name: Cerumen impaction
fields.definition: Cerumen (protective, thick, oily/waxy secretion of the outer third of the external ear canal) fully or partially obstructing the canal, which is usually self-cleansing
fields.etiology: Most commonly self-induced: attempts to clean the ear canal push cerumen deeper into the canal
fields.risk_factors: Inserting objects into the external canal (prevention: insert nothing; wipe the canal opening with a washcloth over the index finger)
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: May be asymptomatic; pruritus; sensation of fullness; conductive hearing loss
fields.diagnosis: Exam: visible cerumen fully or partially obstructing the external canal; may appear wet/sticky, dry/flaky, or dark
fields.treatment: OTC (over-the-counter) otic preparations soften cerumen and speed evacuation; clinic irrigation (body-temperature water, ONLY if the tympanic membrane (TM) is intact) or suction; curette removal (best for soft cerumen and compliant patients, painful if done incorrectly); with tympanostomy tubes or TM perforation, removal by ENT (ear, nose, and throat specialist)

fields.name: Cholesteatoma (keratinoma); acquired (primary, secondary) or congenital
fields.definition: Collection of keratinized squamous epithelium in the middle ear or mastoid; has no cholesterol components and is not a neoplasm
fields.etiology: Primary acquired: forms from tympanic membrane (TM) retraction, commonly the pars flaccida (may involve the pars tensa); secondary acquired: epithelial migration from the TM or after surgery; congenital: forms without TM retraction or perforation; acquired cholesteatoma is a complication of otitis media with effusion
fields.epidemiology: Primary is the most common type; congenital is the least common
fields.risk_factors: Eustachian tube dysfunction; chronic middle ear inflammation
fields.pathology: Squamous epithelium and keratin debris accumulate in a TM retraction or behind the TM; can erode bone and the ossicles
fields.clinical: May be asymptomatic; tinnitus; recurrent otorrhea without otitis externa; hearing loss can be a late finding in primary cholesteatoma; rarely vertigo/dysequilibrium; complications: bone erosion, otorrhea, increased infection risk if middle ear and eustachian tube function are compromised
fields.diagnosis: Usually clinical; exam: TM retraction containing squamous epithelium and keratin debris and/or debris visible behind the TM (congenital: white lesion behind a normal TM), possibly purulent otorrhea, granulation tissue, ossicular erosion; audiometry for hearing loss; CT (computed tomography) for extent of severe cases, useful in secondary acquired disease if the TM is opaque
fields.treatment: Refer to ENT (ear, nose, and throat specialist); remove canal debris; antibiotics for infection; surgical removal, usually with tympanoplasty (reconstruction of the TM and ossicles if necessary); mastoidectomy if it extends into the mastoid with bony erosion

fields.name: Hematoma of the external ear
fields.definition: Pooling of blood in the sub-perichondrial space
fields.etiology: Usually blunt trauma
fields.pathology: Accumulated blood keeps oxygen and nutrients from the cartilage, risking tissue necrosis and deformity from necrosis/chronic scarring; granulation tissue forms after 7 days
fields.clinical: May develop hours after an injury; complications: recurrent/chronic hematoma, cauliflower ear (cosmetic deformity of the auricle)
fields.diagnosis: Early diagnosis essential; exam: edema and ecchymosis of the auricle, loss of cartilaginous landmarks; follow up 12-24 hours after the initial evaluation
fields.treatment: Immediate drainage by incision or large-needle aspiration (harder after 7 days); then irrigation with topical antibiotics and/or systemic antibiotics; ear splinting (cotton bolsters, plaster molds, silicone putty, thermoplastic splints) improves cosmetic outcome and prevents recurrence; recurrent/chronic hematoma needs surgical debridement

conditions.name: Lacerations and avulsion of the ear

fields.name: Lacerations/avulsion of the ear
fields.definition: Not covered in the lecture
fields.etiology: Blunt or sharp trauma
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Prompt repair and infection prevention are critical; simple lacerations closed with sutures; complex lacerations/avulsions may need debridement before closure; tissue grafts if tissue lost; recovered avulsed tissue can often be reattached; cover repairs with a pressure dressing to prevent hematoma

fields.name: Tympanic membrane (TM) perforation; central or marginal
fields.definition: Disruption in the TM: central (does not extend to the margin) or marginal (involves the margin)
fields.etiology: Impact injury; explosive acoustic trauma; barotrauma; severe acute otitis media
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Symptoms vary with cause; generally not painful after the initial rupture; conductive hearing loss; complications: disruption of the ossicles if traumatic, risk of infection
fields.diagnosis: Exam: visible disruption in the TM; drainage through the perforation may be present if associated with acute otitis media
fields.treatment: Most resolve spontaneously over several weeks (as little as 48-72 hours if associated with acute otitis media); surgical TM reconstruction for larger or long-standing perforations (ENT (ear, nose, and throat specialist))

conditions.name: Foreign body of the ear canal

fields.name: Foreign body of the external ear canal
fields.definition: Not covered in the lecture
fields.etiology: Anything that fits into the external canal: beads, popcorn, crayons, insects, pencil erasers, paper, etc.
fields.epidemiology: More common in children than adults, but may occur at any age
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Otalgia varying with the object's shape/structure; bloody discharge if the canal lining is damaged; sensation of fullness or foreign body
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Do not push the object deeper; ENT (ear, nose, and throat specialist) referral for removal under microscopy may be warranted; firm objects: loop or hook; soft objects: alligator forceps; irrigation with caution (organic objects swell when wet) and only if the tympanic membrane (TM) is known intact; immobilize insects by filling the canal with lidocaine first (only if TM intact)

fields.name: Foreign body of the auricle (embedded piercing)
fields.definition: Piercing embedded in the earlobe or another part of the auricle
fields.etiology: Ear piercings
fields.epidemiology: Most common in girls and young adolescents with pierced ears, but may occur at any age
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Pain, erythema, and edema of the affected area; possible purulent drainage from the piercing site
fields.diagnosis: Exam: pain on palpation of the affected area; foreign body may be palpable
fields.treatment: Removal of the object under local anesthetic; younger or non-compliant patients may need sedation; infection is the biggest concern

fields.name: Otitis externa (OE); acute and chronic OE
fields.definition: Inflammation and infection of the external canal
fields.etiology: Most commonly Pseudomonas aeruginosa (38%), Staphylococcus epidermidis (9%), Staphylococcus aureus (8%); also other bacteria and fungi (otomycosis)
fields.epidemiology: Affects 10% of people in their lifetime; all age groups, most common in children and early adolescence; most common in summer months
fields.risk_factors: Moisture (swimming/water exposure); epithelial damage (aggressive cleaning/scratching); foreign bodies (cotton swab particles, paper); canal occlusion (hearing aids, headphones); auricular dermatitis (hygiene products, metal jewelry, psoriasis, atopic dermatitis); radiation therapy
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Varies with duration and degree; otalgia worse with touch or movement of the auricle/tragus; otorrhea; pruritus; fullness; decreased hearing; complication: malignant (necrotizing) external otitis
fields.diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis; exam: tenderness, canal discharge, canal erythema/edema (erythema common in chronic OE), periauricular and anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, skin thickening in chronic OE; cultures only if severe, chronic, recurrent, immunosuppressed, postoperative, or treatment failure; differential: otomycosis, suppurative otitis media, contact dermatitis, psoriasis, ear canal carcinoma (rare)
fields.treatment: Debris removal; otic drops: antiseptic (e.g., boric acid, aluminum acetate, alcohol), antibiotic (e.g., ofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, neomycin, polymyxin B), acidifying (acetic acid), combinations with steroids to reduce pain/inflammation; ear wick if canal stenosis; avoid acidifying and aminoglycoside drops if the tympanic membrane may not be intact

fields.name: Malignant external otitis; necrotizing external otitis
fields.definition: Severe infection of the bone/marrow spaces of the skull base and the soft tissue/cartilage of the temporal region; a complication of otitis externa
fields.etiology: Most commonly spread of Pseudomonas aeruginosa from otitis externa (>95%)
fields.epidemiology: Elderly patients with diabetes and immunocompromised patients are most at risk
fields.risk_factors: Diabetes in the elderly; immunocompromise; preceding otitis externa
fields.pathology: Infection spreads from the external canal into skull-base bone and marrow and temporal soft tissue/cartilage; may cause visible necrosis of the ear canal
fields.clinical: Severe otalgia out of proportion to exam findings; copious otorrhea; possible visible ear canal necrosis; facial nerve weakness
fields.diagnosis: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) or CT (computed tomography) shows infection in bony structures
fields.treatment: Antipseudomonal antibiotics (e.g., ciprofloxacin)

fields.name: Otomycosis (fungal otitis externa)
fields.definition: Fungal infection of the external canal
fields.etiology: Most commonly Aspergillus niger and Candida
fields.epidemiology: 9% of ear canal infections; varies with climate
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Pruritus; discomfort (less painful than bacterial otitis externa); otorrhea; foreign body sensation
fields.diagnosis: Exam: Aspergillus shows visible fungal spores/filaments ("wet newspaper" appearance); Candida shows white fluffy/curd-like material; mild-moderate edema; on the otitis externa differential
fields.treatment: Debris removal; topical antifungals

fields.name: Otosclerosis
fields.definition: Bony overgrowth affecting the stapes, leading to eventual fixation and hearing loss
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Bony overgrowth at the stapes causes stapes fixation and conductive hearing loss
fields.clinical: Gradually progressive conductive hearing loss, bilateral and asymmetric (70%) or unilateral (30%); hears better with background noise; tinnitus
fields.diagnosis: Otoscopy normal (excludes other conductive causes such as foreign body, cerumen); Weber (lateralizes to the affected ear, or the more affected ear if bilateral) and Rinne (bone conduction ≥ air conduction) consistent with conductive loss; audiometry for extent; CT (computed tomography) is the initial imaging of choice; differential: tympanic membrane perforation, tympanosclerosis, otitis media with effusion, cholesteatoma, ossicular discontinuity, middle ear tumor
fields.treatment: Observation if unilateral or not bothered; hearing aids; elective surgery one ear at a time: stapes replacement with a prosthesis or cochlear implant (ENT (ear, nose, and throat specialist)); sodium fluoride and bisphosphonates under investigation, use varies (ENT)

fields.name: Keloid of the ear (benign neoplasm of the ear)
fields.definition: Hypertrophic scars (deck's wording), a benign neoplasm of the ear
fields.etiology: Result from trauma
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Pictured as large rounded scar masses on the earlobe and auricle
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Avoid trauma; intralesional steroid injection; corticosteroid tape; excision; radiation therapy in adults, NEVER in children; follow closely for recurrence

fields.name: Carcinoma of the ear canal (malignant neoplasm of the ear)
fields.definition: Malignant neoplasm of the ear canal
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Aggressive malignant growth in the ear canal
fields.clinical: Abnormal growth in the ear canal; bloody otorrhea; friable ear canal; failure to respond to treatment for external otitis; late findings: hearing loss and facial paralysis
fields.diagnosis: Definitive diagnosis by biopsy; often misdiagnosed as external otitis; on the otitis externa differential
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

lectures.deck: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx
lectures.note: Mastoiditis is listed in the instructional objectives (slide 2) but is not taught anywhere in this deck. Cholesteatoma, foreign body, tympanic membrane perforation, and multiple sclerosis appear only as names in cause lists.

conditions.name: Conductive hearing loss
conditions.prof_note: Speaker notes on slide 11 (conductive causes list) mark it 'IMPORTANT'

fields.name: Conductive hearing loss (CHL)
fields.definition: Hearing loss from dysfunction of the external/middle ear that impairs conduction of sound vibration to the inner ear
fields.etiology: Obstruction (cerumen); mass loading (effusion); stiffness (otosclerosis); discontinuity (ossicular disruption); causes: cerumen impaction and eustachian tube dysfunction (most common in adults), otitis media, tympanic membrane (TM) perforation, otosclerosis, foreign body, mass lesions (cholesteatoma, exostosis, glomus tumors), ossicular chain discontinuity
fields.epidemiology: Most common onset in childhood and young adulthood, up to age 40 (loss from cerumen impaction can occur beyond 40)
fields.pathology: External or middle ear disorder impairs sound conduction to the inner ear; inner ear and cochlear nerve intact
fields.clinical: Ear canal/TM abnormality usually visible (except otosclerosis); little effect on sound; hearing seems to improve in noisy environments; voice remains soft
fields.diagnosis: Weber: lateralizes to the impaired ear; Rinne: bone conduction (BC) = air conduction (AC) or BC > AC; tympanometry assesses middle ear/TM mobility and ossicular continuity
fields.treatment: Often correctable

fields.name: Cerumen impaction
fields.definition: Obstruction of the ear canal by cerumen, a cause of conductive hearing loss
fields.etiology: Obstruction by cerumen
fields.epidemiology: One of the most common causes of conductive hearing loss in adults; can occur beyond age 40
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Otitis media; otitis media with effusion
fields.definition: Middle ear fluid accumulation (effusion) causing conductive hearing loss by mass loading of the eardrum
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Mass loading: fluid adds weight to the tympanic membrane, altering acoustic properties and dampening sound conduction; stiff middle ear system
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Tympanogram type B (little or no point of maximum mobility, reduced compliance; flat curve)
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

conditions.name: Otosclerosis
conditions.prof_note: Speaker notes on slide 28 (type As tympanogram in otosclerosis) mark it 'IMPORTANT'

fields.name: Otosclerosis
fields.definition: Abnormal bone growth in the middle ear that fixes the stapes in place, preventing it from vibrating
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Stiffness effect: fixed stapes/ossicular chain cannot vibrate, causing progressive conductive hearing loss
fields.clinical: Progressive conductive hearing loss; ear canal and tympanic membrane (TM) usually look normal (exception among conductive causes)
fields.diagnosis: Tympanogram type As (normal middle ear pressure with a reduced compliance peak, from ossicular chain fixation)
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Ossicular chain discontinuity (ossicular chain disruption)
fields.definition: Separation or dislocation of the malleus, incus, and stapes, stopping sound from traveling correctly to the inner ear
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Discontinuity of the ossicular chain interrupts sound conduction (conductive hearing loss)
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Tympanogram type Ad (normal middle ear pressure with hypermobility; flaccid tympanic membrane from ossicular disarticulation); tympanometry estimates ossicular chain continuity
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

conditions.name: Eustachian tube dysfunction
conditions.prof_note: Speaker notes on slide 11 mark it 'IMPORTANT' (followed by the ETD note); slide 27 notes mark type C 'IMPORTANT'

fields.name: Eustachian tube dysfunction (ETD)
fields.definition: Not covered in the lecture
fields.etiology: Transient ETD secondary to upper respiratory infection; inflammation, infection, or mass lesion
fields.epidemiology: One of the most common causes of conductive hearing loss in adults
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: A negative tympanogram pressure peak almost invariably indicates ETD; type C tympanogram (maximal compliance at significant negative middle ear pressure; treatment-significant when more negative than -200 mm H2O)
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

conditions.name: Sensorineural hearing loss
conditions.prof_note: Speaker notes on slide 14 (SNHL causes list) mark it 'IMPORTANT'

fields.name: Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL); sensory and neural hearing loss grouped together
fields.definition: Sensory: deterioration of the cochlea and loss of hair cells; neural: lesions of cranial nerve 8, auditory nuclei, ascending tracts, or auditory cortex
fields.etiology: Presbycusis (most common), noise, head trauma, Ménière's disease, ototoxicity, developmental/hereditary, multiple sclerosis, idiopathic, labyrinthitis, perilymphatic fistula, vascular (hypercoagulation, diabetes mellitus), syphilis, autoimmune disorders, acoustic neuroma
fields.epidemiology: Most common onset in middle or later years
fields.pathology: Inner ear disorder involving the cochlear nerve and neuronal impulse transmission to the brain
fields.clinical: Trouble hearing on the phone, in groups/crowded rooms, the TV, doorbell, phone ring; 'people seem to mumble'; higher registers lost so sound may be distorted; worse in noise; voice may be loud; ear canal/tympanic membrane normal
fields.diagnosis: Weber: lateralizes to the good ear; Rinne: air conduction > bone conduction; type A tympanogram; labs usually unnecessary except syphilis testing; vestibular testing an adjunct in selected patients; MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) with gadolinium for suspected retrocochlear loss
fields.treatment: Usually not correctable; may be stabilized; some types preventable; acute-onset sensory loss may respond to corticosteroids in the first weeks

fields.name: Tinnitus
fields.definition: Hearing a sound (ringing, buzzing, roaring) when no external sound is present
fields.etiology: Can be associated with any type of hearing loss
fields.risk_factors: Low tolerance for normal 'head' noise with depression, neurosis, stress, fatigue (fatigue a significant contributing risk factor)
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Ringing, buzzing, humming, hissing, motor running, insects; often the first symptom of hearing loss; usually subjective, occasionally objective (heard by the examiner too); red flag: unilateral, pulsatile
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: No drug more effective than placebo; biofeedback, masking noises; avoid loud noise and stimulants, check lead level, daily exercise, adequate rest, learn to ignore the noise

fields.name: Exostosis (surfer's ear)
fields.definition: Bony growth in the external ear canal
fields.etiology: Repetitive exposure to cold water
fields.pathology: Benign bony growth projecting from the bone surface; bilaterally symmetrical
fields.clinical: Can block the canal or collect debris; conductive hearing loss
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Glomus tumor
fields.definition: Benign, highly vascular tumor derived from normal glomus formations of the middle ear and jugular bulb
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Middle ear mass effect; may cause bony destruction of the skull
fields.clinical: Conductive hearing loss; pulsatile tinnitus; can present with spontaneous hemorrhage and paralysis of cranial nerves IX, X, XI
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Ototoxicity (drug toxicity)
fields.definition: Drug-induced damage to hearing (and balance)
fields.etiology: Aminoglycosides (most ototoxic and common), furosemide/loop diuretics, aspirin/salicylates, platinum-based chemotherapy, alcohol; many other agents
fields.risk_factors: Ototoxic drugs are often also nephrotoxic and vice versa (including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs)
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss; peripheral vertigo of insidious or acute onset with nausea, vomiting; tinnitus may be present
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Monitor aminoglycoside peak levels
fields.mortality: Prognosis: may or may not be reversible; partial adaptation occurs

fields.name: Noise-induced sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL)
fields.definition: SNHL from noise exposure, temporary or permanent
fields.etiology: Loud or repeated noise exposure; rarely, extremely intense impulse noise perforates the tympanic membrane (conductive hearing loss)
fields.epidemiology: One of the most common occupationally induced disabilities; exposure regulated by OSHA (Occupational Safety and Health Administration)
fields.risk_factors: Noise level high enough or repeated often enough; damage possible after 2 hours at 80-85 dB (decibels), under 5 minutes at 105-110 dB
fields.pathology: Temporary threshold shift (TTS: temporary SNHL after acute exposure); permanent threshold shift (PTS: permanent loss after high or repeated exposure)
fields.clinical: Ear feels full, 'crickets' after acute exposure
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture
fields.mortality: Prognosis: most acute exposures recover in 24-48 hours; high-level or repeated exposure causes permanent loss

fields.name: Traumatic hearing loss: acoustic trauma; blows to the head; penetrating injuries
fields.definition: Hearing loss from a single loud noise (acoustic trauma), head blows, or penetrating ear injury
fields.etiology: Single loud noise; tympanic membrane perforation; blows to the head (labyrinthine injury); penetrating injuries (stapes subluxation)
fields.pathology: Head blows can cause labyrinthine injury with sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL); penetrating injury usually subluxates the stapes, causing profound SNHL
fields.clinical: Immediate hearing loss after acoustic trauma; may mimic noise-induced loss or be complete loss of auditory and vestibular function
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Barotrauma
fields.definition: Injury of the tympanic membrane (TM) and middle ear caused by unequalized pressure
fields.etiology: Unequalized pressure during flying or underwater diving
fields.pathology: Pressure injury to TM/middle ear; may be followed by hemotympanum (blood in the middle ear) or transudative middle ear effusion
fields.clinical: Pain, hyperemia, TM perforation, edema, ecchymosis; may result in conductive hearing loss
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

conditions.name: Presbycusis
conditions.prof_note: Speaker notes on slide 14 (which define presbycusis, marked most common) mark it 'IMPORTANT'

fields.name: Presbycusis
fields.definition: Gradual, progressive, age-related hearing loss in both ears
fields.etiology: Aging
fields.epidemiology: Most common cause of sensorineural hearing loss; age is the strongest predictor of hearing loss
fields.pathology: Deterioration/loss of hair cells in the organ of Corti and cochlear nerve degeneration; sensorineural
fields.clinical: Bilateral, symmetric, gradual loss; high frequencies first, progressing to mid-low; can hear speech but can't make out words; misses doorbell/phone; may have tinnitus; lip reads
fields.diagnosis: Audiogram: sloping high-frequency hearing loss
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Perilymphatic fistula
fields.definition: Pathologic communication between the perilymphatic space of the inner ear and the middle ear, at the round or oval window
fields.etiology: Congenital or acquired; acquired from barotrauma, temporal bone trauma, or stapedectomy complication
fields.epidemiology: Rare cause of vertigo and sensorineural hearing loss
fields.risk_factors: Head injury, barotrauma, heavy lifting and straining, stapedectomy
fields.pathology: Fistula at the round or oval window
fields.clinical: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo after head injury, barotrauma, or straining; sometimes an audible 'pop'
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Treat symptomatically and refer to ENT (ear, nose, and throat specialist)

fields.name: Autoimmune sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL)
fields.definition: SNHL from systemic autoimmune disorders
fields.etiology: Uncommon: Cogan's syndrome, polyarteritis nodosa, relapsing polychondritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's); rarer: scleroderma, temporal arteritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Most often bilateral and progressive SNHL with periods of deterioration and stabilization; may have vestibular dysfunction
fields.diagnosis: Routine screening for autoimmune disorders does not appear warranted
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome)-related sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL)
fields.definition: SNHL as one of the many neurologic manifestations of AIDS
fields.etiology: Infectious complication (cryptococcal meningitis, syphilis) or primary neurologic manifestation
fields.risk_factors: Consider when AIDS risk factors are present
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Unexplained SNHL
fields.diagnosis: Consider AIDS in unexplained SNHL if risk factors present
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Syphilitic sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL)
fields.definition: Congenital or acquired SNHL from syphilis
fields.etiology: Syphilis (Treponema pallidum), congenital or acquired
fields.epidemiology: Hearing loss up to 80% in symptomatic neurosyphilis; not associated with primary acquired syphilis
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Often indistinguishable from Ménière's: fluctuating SNHL, tinnitus, aural fullness, episodic vertigo
fields.diagnosis: FTA-ABS (fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption) and MHA-TP (microhemagglutination test for Treponema pallidum) should be obtained; VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) not helpful
fields.treatment: Antibiotic plus systemic corticosteroids; important to manage as a potentially treatable cause of SNHL

fields.name: Ménière's disease
fields.definition: Peripheral vestibular disorder of episodic vertigo with fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), tinnitus, and aural fullness
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Episodic spontaneous severe spinning vertigo lasting hours (often presenting complaint), with nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis, nystagmus; fluctuating then progressive low-frequency SNHL; low-tone 'blowing' tinnitus; unilateral ear fullness
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Hereditary sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL)
fields.definition: Inherited SNHL, nonsyndromic or syndromic
fields.etiology: Nonsyndromic hereditary hearing loss; Waardenburg's syndrome; Alport syndrome; Usher's syndrome
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

conditions.name: Acoustic neuroma
conditions.prof_note: Speaker notes on slide 74 mark 'IMPORTANT - Slow growing'

fields.name: Acoustic neuroma
fields.definition: Rare, slow-growing benign tumor of cranial nerve (CN) VIII, arising from sheath cells of its vestibular component
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Benign, slow-growing tumor from sheath cells of the vestibular branch of CN VIII; causes CN VIII compression; may involve CN V and VII
fields.clinical: Unilateral hearing loss (may be sudden); poor speech discrimination for the degree of tone loss; disequilibrium; tinnitus
fields.diagnosis: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) with gadolinium is the gold standard for retrocochlear loss; electronystagmography is the gold standard for one-ear disorders; ipsilateral vestibular hypofunction with unilateral progressive SNHL (sensorineural hearing loss) suggests retrocochlear lesion
fields.treatment: Observation (annual MRI), surgery, or radiation
fields.mortality: Prognosis: progression may not be so 'benign'

fields.name: Vertebrobasilar arterial insufficiency/occlusion (vertebrobasilar artery disease)
fields.definition: Not covered in the lecture
fields.etiology: Thrombotic or embolic occlusion; atherosclerosis or cervical arthritis
fields.epidemiology: Common cause of vertigo in elderly patients
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Acute vertigo, nausea/vomiting, facial paralysis, tinnitus, ipsilateral gaze paralysis, ipsilateral facial and contralateral trunk/limb loss of pain and temperature, ipsilateral Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis)
fields.diagnosis: MRA (magnetic resonance angiography)
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture
fields.mortality: Complications: can lead to TIAs (transient ischemic attacks) and CVAs (cerebral vascular accidents)

fields.name: Isolated cerebellar infarction
fields.definition: Not covered in the lecture
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Vertigo, facial pain or numbness, headache, or ataxia
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Refer for evaluation (don't miss something bigger than the hearing loss)

fields.name: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL)
fields.definition: Unilateral sudden SNHL; a syndrome, not a disease
fields.etiology: Viral or vascular; exact etiology rarely certain; rarely retrocochlear pathology
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Unilateral sudden hearing loss
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Prompt referral to ENT (ear, nose, and throat specialist); acute-onset sensory loss may respond to corticosteroids in the first weeks

fields.name: Functional hearing loss
fields.definition: Not covered in the lecture
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Inconsistencies, complaints, and exaggerated listening effort on history; claimed bilateral significant loss with normal voice level and articulation
fields.diagnosis: History and voice/speech quality; suspect functional behavior when claimed bilateral loss coexists with normal voice and articulation
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Vascular disorders causing dizziness: small vessel ischemic disease; carotid artery stenosis
fields.definition: Most common non-vestibular cause of dizziness and balance loss in the elderly
fields.etiology: Small vessel ischemic disease (atherosclerosis) most common; carotid artery stenosis
fields.epidemiology: Elderly; carotid stenosis common, frequently with other peripheral vascular disorders
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Increased reflex time; difficulty processing complex tasks, balance, and locomotion; syncope
fields.diagnosis: MRA (magnetic resonance angiography), showing small white lesions in small vessel disease; noninvasive carotid studies (Doppler)
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture
fields.mortality: Complications: can lead to TIAs (transient ischemic attacks) and CVAs (cerebral vascular accidents)

fields.name: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
fields.definition: Severe vertigo associated with a change in head position
fields.etiology: Most cases have no identifiable cause; canalithiasis of the posterior semicircular canal thought most frequent (deck labels it 'cupulolithiasis theory')
fields.pathology: Displaced otoliths in the semicircular canal (posterior canal most frequent)
fields.clinical: Vertigo after 10-15 second latency lasting 10-60 seconds (>1 minute: consider another diagnosis) when rolling over, getting in/out of bed, looking up, tilting head back; specific side; clustered bouts; imbalance, worse on awakening; nausea, vomiting, nystagmus; hearing and tinnitus unaffected
fields.diagnosis: Classic eye movements on Dix-Hallpike maneuver (positional test provoking nystagmus) plus suggestive history; electronystagmography may be used
fields.treatment: Epley maneuver (repositions otoliths in the semicircular canal)
fields.mortality: Prognosis: bouts separated by remissions of months or more; episodes last a few weeks and may recur

fields.name: Labyrinthitis
fields.definition: Inflammation of the membranous labyrinth of the inner ear
fields.etiology: Evidence supports viral cause; could be bacterial infection or systemic autoimmune disease; exact cause rarely certain
fields.pathology: Inflammation of the membranous labyrinth
fields.clinical: Relatively sudden onset of sensorineural hearing loss and acute vertigo lasting several days to weeks; fever if bacterial
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Symptomatic; antibiotics if bacterial infection signs (fever); oral corticosteroids; oral diazepam or meclizine during acute vertigo

fields.name: Vestibular neuronitis (vestibular neuritis)
fields.definition: Inflammation of the vestibular portion of cranial nerve 8
fields.etiology: Likely viral; exact cause unknown
fields.pathology: Inflammation of the vestibular portion of cranial nerve 8
fields.clinical: Dramatic sudden vertigo, nausea, vomiting, nystagmus, gait imbalance; dizziness lasts days with gradual improvement; balance symptoms for months; no hearing change, tinnitus, or focal neurologic complaints
fields.diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis; electronystagmography is the gold standard for one-ear disorders
fields.treatment: Symptomatic: oral diazepam or meclizine during acute vertigo; antiemetics; oral corticosteroids (deck marks with '?')
fields.mortality: Prognosis: considered benign, self-limiting; may recur over 12-18 months

lectures.title: Disorders of the Nose and Paranasal Sinuses

fields.name: Acute sinusitis; acute rhinosinusitis (preferred term, because rhinitis and sinusitis usually coexist)
fields.definition: Symptomatic inflammation of one or more paranasal sinuses lasting <4 weeks, from impaired drainage and retained secretions, with obstruction, facial pain/pressure/fullness, or both
fields.etiology: Infectious and noninfectious causes that obstruct the sinus ostia and retain mucus; viral in 90–98% (rhinovirus, parainfluenza virus, influenza virus); bacterial less often; fungal (Rhizopus, Mucor, occasionally Aspergillus) in immunocompromised patients; noninfectious: allergic rhinitis, barotrauma, chemical irritants
fields.epidemiology: Affects 1 in 8 adults (>30 million diagnosed with rhinosinusitis in the US each year); sinuses most often infected: maxillary > ethmoid > frontal > sphenoid
fields.risk_factors: Chronic allergies; smoking; immunocompromise; anatomical defect
fields.pathology: Allergy/infection/inflammation → structural abnormality or mucosal congestion → obstruction of the ostiomeatal complex or sinus ostia → sinus hypoxia, mucosal edema, reduced mucociliary clearance, pooled secretions; maxillary sinuses most infected because their ostia are accessible to the outside
fields.clinical: Nasal drainage/congestion (rhinorrhea, postnasal drip), facial pain or pressure, headache; associated retro-orbital pain, otalgia, hyposmia, halitosis, chronic cough; viral cause gives a viral syndrome; urgent: visual disturbance (especially diplopia), periorbital swelling or erythema, altered mental status
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; tests not routinely recommended and none separate viral from bacterial; ≥3 clinical findings match imaging accuracy, so routine sinus radiography is discouraged; limited coronal CT (computed tomography) for recurrence or treatment failure; sinus CT if extrasinus involvement suspected
fields.treatment: Most improve without antibiotics; symptomatic: decongestants, NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), nasal/sinus saline irrigation (neti pot, saline sprays), intranasal steroids; oseltamivir if influenza (age >13); ENT (ear, nose, and throat) referral for surgery if medical treatment fails; educate on diagnosis, cause, device/medication use, referral

fields.name: Acute bacterial sinusitis; acute bacterial rhinosinusitis
fields.definition: Acute sinusitis caused by bacterial infection of stagnant sinus secretions, often a bacterial superinfection of viral rhinosinusitis
fields.etiology: Streptococcus pneumoniae, nontypable Haemophilus influenzae, and (in children) Moraxella catarrhalis; nosocomial cases often polymicrobial with Staphylococcus aureus and gram-negative bacilli
fields.epidemiology: Bacterial superinfection in 0.5–2% of viral rhinosinusitis episodes; diagnosis is the fifth leading reason for prescribing antibiotics
fields.risk_factors: Chronic allergies, smoking, immunocompromise, anatomical defect (acute sinusitis); antibiotic exposure within 30 days or >30% local penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae changes antibiotic choice
fields.pathology: Ostial obstruction → pooled, stagnant secretions → bacterial infection; if unresolved it can become chronic sinusitis
fields.clinical: Worsening >5–6 days after initial improvement; symptoms ≥10 days; persistent purulent discharge; unilateral upper tooth/facial pain; unilateral maxillary tenderness; fever (>100.4 F) and severe pain reproducible on palpation, worse bending over or supine; tooth pain, halitosis, tearing, odynophagia; yellow and putrid discharge; rust-colored discharge suggests Streptococcus pneumoniae
fields.diagnosis: Clinical (no test separates viral from bacterial); confirm fever is not masked by antipyretics; CT (computed tomography) for recurrence, treatment failure, or suspected extrasinus involvement
fields.treatment: Symptomatic care + antibiotics: amoxicillin/clavulanate; penicillin allergy: doxycycline or an antipneumococcal fluoroquinolone (moxifloxacin); recent antibiotics or resistance risk: extended-release amoxicillin/clavulanate, doxycycline, or fluoroquinolone; treatment failure: extended-release amoxicillin/clavulanate or fluoroquinolone; ENT (ear, nose, and throat) referral for surgery if medical treatment fails

fields.name: Allergic sinusitis
fields.definition: Allergy-driven sinus symptoms: allergies do not cause inflammation (-itis) per se but create the environment for infection; many patients who believe they have sinusitis actually have allergic sinusitis
fields.etiology: Allergic rhinitis (a noninfectious cause of sinusitis)
fields.pathology: Multiple pathophysiology pathways
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: 80% of patients use 2 or more allergy medications: non-drowsy oral antihistamine (loratadine, fexofenadine, cetirizine, levocetirizine; drowsy ones at night); leukotriene inhibitor at night (zafirlukast, montelukast); intranasal steroid (fluticasone; caution with chronic use); intranasal ipratropium; immunotherapy; decongestants (caution with chronic use and high blood pressure); local honey

fields.name: Chronic sinusitis; chronic bacterial sinusitis
fields.definition: Sinusitis lasting >12 weeks
fields.etiology: Commonly associated with bacterial or fungal infection
fields.pathology: Impaired mucociliary clearance → repeated infections rather than one persistent infection; unresolved obstruction/infection progresses to chronic sinusitis
fields.clinical: Constant nasal congestion and sinus pressure with periods of increased severity
fields.diagnosis: Sinus CT (computed tomography) defines extent, detects an anatomic defect or obstruction, and tracks response; endoscopic tissue samples for histology and culture; consider CBC (complete blood count) with differential and IgE (immunoglobulin E); allergy skin testing referral
fields.treatment: Repeated antibiotic courses (often 3–4 weeks at a time); intranasal glucocorticoids, sinus irrigation; oral steroids plus two weeks of amoxicillin/clavulanate; ENT (ear, nose, and throat) referral for surgical evaluation

fields.name: Chronic fungal sinusitis; mycetoma (fungus ball) form
fields.definition: Noninvasive chronic fungal sinus disease in immunocompetent hosts
fields.etiology: Typically Aspergillus and dematiaceous molds
fields.pathology: Noninvasive; may form a mycetoma (fungus ball) in a sinus, which can erode bone
fields.clinical: Usually mild and indolent; mycetoma presents as unilateral disease
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Mild indolent disease: endoscopic surgery, usually without antifungals; mycetoma: surgery, plus antifungals if bony erosion; recurrence is common

fields.name: Allergic fungal sinusitis (AFS)
fields.definition: Allergic form of chronic fungal sinusitis presenting as pansinusitis with thick eosinophil-laden mucus
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Seen in patients with nasal polyps and asthma; nasal polyps occur in 85% of patients with AFS (allergic fungal sinusitis)
fields.pathology: Thick, eosinophil-laden mucus
fields.clinical: Pansinusitis with mucus the consistency of peanut butter; multiple nasal polyps (including in children)
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Deviated (nasal) septum
fields.definition: Nasal septum significantly displaced to one side, making one nasal air passage smaller than the other
fields.etiology: Congenital or traumatic
fields.pathology: Displacement narrows one airway and can block the sinus ostia
fields.clinical: Congestion (ostial blockage) up to anosmia; severe forms: obstructive sleep apnea, snoring, facial pain, recurrent nosebleeds
fields.diagnosis: Seen on coronal CT (computed tomography) and nasal endoscopy (labeled images)
fields.treatment: Surgery: septoplasty by an otorhinolaryngologist

fields.name: Perforated (nasal) septum; septal perforation
fields.definition: Perforation through the nasal septum
fields.etiology: Congenital or traumatic; often intranasal steroid use or cocaine use; rarely Wegener's granulomatosis (a vascular autoimmune disease); rarely secondary syphilis
fields.pathology: Chronic ischemia of the septum (intranasal steroids, cocaine)
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Physical examination, possibly CT (computed tomography)
fields.treatment: Treat the underlying cause (septum may heal); otherwise surgery (septoplasty); ENT (ear, nose, and throat) referral

fields.name: Septal hematoma
fields.definition: Hematoma between the nasal septum and the perichondrium/mucosal epithelium
fields.etiology: Usually trauma; also bleeding disorders, cocaine, foreign body, medications
fields.pathology: Blood collects between septal cartilage and perichondrium
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Drainage via intranasal incision under general anesthesia (illustrated incision, evacuation, and packing)

fields.name: Anterior epistaxis (anterior nosebleed)
fields.definition: Nosebleed from an anterior source; by far the most common type
fields.etiology: Most common: trauma from the patient's finger; 90% arise in Kiesselbach's plexus (vascular watershed area of the anterior septum)
fields.epidemiology: Common emergency department complaint; most cases before age 10 or at 45–65 years; winter predominance
fields.risk_factors: Chronic dry nose; anticoagulant use; hemophilia; coagulation disorders; tumors; recent trauma or surgery; medications (aspirin, warfarin, clopidogrel, intranasal glucocorticoids); cirrhosis; HIV (human immunodeficiency virus); intranasal cocaine
fields.pathology: Cracked mucosa with damaged vessels in Kiesselbach's plexus
fields.clinical: Nasal bleeding; symptoms of blood loss (chest discomfort, dyspnea, lightheadedness) and worsening of coronary artery disease or COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease)
fields.diagnosis: ABC (airway, breathing, circulation) first; normal appearance, vital signs, and respiratory function are reassuring; determine anterior vs posterior; history of timing, frequency, severity, predisposing conditions; PT (prothrombin time)/INR (international normalized ratio) only if anticoagulated; hematocrit and type and crossmatch if massive or prolonged
fields.treatment: Blow nose to clear clots, oxymetazoline spray, pinch alae against septum continuously 10 minutes; sit leaning forward, cotton pledget (± antibiotic ointment), spit out blood, cold compress to bridge (teach for home); then nasal tampons, gauze packing, balloon catheters, thrombogenic foams/gels; do not blow nose; ENT (ear, nose, and throat) referral

fields.name: Posterior epistaxis (posterior nosebleed)
fields.definition: Nosebleed from a posterior source, most often the posterolateral branches of the sphenopalatine artery, sometimes carotid branches
fields.etiology: Posterolateral branches of the sphenopalatine artery; branches of the carotid artery
fields.epidemiology: Less common than anterior bleeds; epistaxis overall peaks before age 10 and at 45–65 years, in winter
fields.risk_factors: Chronic dry nose; anticoagulant use; hemophilia; coagulation disorders; tumors; recent trauma or surgery; medications (aspirin, warfarin, clopidogrel, intranasal glucocorticoids); cirrhosis; HIV (human immunodeficiency virus); intranasal cocaine
fields.pathology: Arterial bleeding that can produce significant hemorrhage
fields.clinical: Significant hemorrhage; symptoms of blood loss (chest discomfort, dyspnea, lightheadedness)
fields.diagnosis: ABC (airway, breathing, circulation) first; normal appearance, vital signs, and respiratory function are reassuring; determine anterior vs posterior; history of timing, frequency, severity, predisposing conditions; PT (prothrombin time)/INR (international normalized ratio) only if anticoagulated; hematocrit and type and crossmatch if massive or prolonged
fields.treatment: Initial tamponade (clear clots, oxymetazoline, 10 minutes of pressure); nasal packing for severe nosebleeds, balloon catheters, thrombogenic foams/gels; two large-bore IV (intravenous) lines if massive; do not blow nose; ENT (ear, nose, and throat) referral
fields.mortality: Prognosis: higher-risk bleed: aspiration risk, possible infection, significant hemorrhage

fields.name: Nasal foreign body (FB)
fields.definition: Not covered in the lecture
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Usually on the nasal floor just under the inferior turbinate, or superiorly just in front of the middle turbinate
fields.clinical: Unilateral purulent, foul-smelling nasal discharge in a young child strongly suggests it
fields.diagnosis: Visualization of the FB (foreign body) establishes the diagnosis; imaging rarely needed
fields.treatment: Removal: Tobey or bayonet forceps for graspable objects (paper, toy part, cotton, foam); wire loop, right-angle hook, curette, or suction tip for nongraspable round/smooth objects (bead, bean, magnet, battery); get help, ENT (ear, nose, and throat) referral

fields.name: Nasal fracture (nasal bridge fracture)
fields.definition: Not covered in the lecture
fields.etiology: Trauma
fields.pathology: Nasal bridge is the most common site; associated with septal hematomas; may accompany orbital or midface fractures
fields.clinical: Contusion/tenderness over the nasal bridge (= fracture); tenderness, crepitus, abnormal movement
fields.diagnosis: Palpation and inspection with a nasal speculum; suspect orbital/midface fractures; no x-ray needed if tenderness/swelling isolated to the bony bridge, breathing through each naris, nose straight, and no septal hematoma; otherwise plain nasal x-rays
fields.treatment: Ice and head-of-bed elevation; if displaced, ENT (ear, nose, and throat) within 8 hours to reset, though waiting 3–4 days for swelling is common

fields.name: Nasal polyps (nasal polyposis)
fields.definition: Abnormal gray, glistening masses filled with inflammatory material in the nasal cavity or paranasal sinuses
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Asthma in 20–50% and aspirin intolerance in 8–26% of polyp patients; polyps in 6–44% of CF (cystic fibrosis), 85% of allergic fungal sinusitis, 50% of Churg-Strauss syndrome, 20% of NARES (nonallergic rhinitis with eosinophilia syndrome); multiple polyps can occur in children with chronic sinusitis, allergic rhinitis, CF, or allergic fungal sinusitis
fields.risk_factors: Chronic rhinosinusitis, asthma, aspirin sensitivity (AERD, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease), allergic rhinitis, CF, allergic fungal sinusitis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, alcohol intolerance, Churg-Strauss syndrome, Young syndrome (chronic sinusitis, nasal polyposis, azoospermia), NARES
fields.pathology: Inflammatory masses, typically seen under the middle turbinate
fields.clinical: Large or extensive polyps: nasal congestion or blockage, thick discharge, anosmia
fields.diagnosis: Characteristic appearance with nasal speculum or rhinoscope; CT (computed tomography) for extent/surgical planning; sweat chloride test if CF concern; CBC (complete blood count) with differential, IgE (immunoglobulin E), IgA (immunoglobulin A); consider nasal smear for eosinophils; evaluate all children with multiple polyps for CF and asthma
fields.treatment: Non-drowsy antihistamine (loratadine, fexofenadine, cetirizine, levocetirizine), leukotriene inhibitor at night (zafirlukast, montelukast), intranasal or oral steroids by extent, intranasal ipratropium, immunotherapy, decongestants (caution); surgery gives temporary relief, polyps often recur in months to years

fields.name: Allergic rhinitis
fields.definition: Rhinorrhea secondary to an allergy
fields.etiology: Allergen (antigen) exposure recognized as foreign
fields.epidemiology: Extremely common and, like all allergy issues, on the rise
fields.pathology: Allergen recognized as foreign → chemokine release → mucus hyperproduction → rhinorrhea
fields.clinical: Clear discharge from each nostril; bluish, edematous nasal mucosa; ± nasal polyps
fields.diagnosis: Clinical, mostly patient history, with the exam findings above
fields.treatment: Often 2 or more medications: non-drowsy antihistamine (loratadine, fexofenadine, cetirizine, levocetirizine; drowsy ones at night), leukotriene inhibitor at night (zafirlukast, montelukast), intranasal steroids (caution chronic use), intranasal ipratropium, immunotherapy, decongestants (caution chronic use and high blood pressure)

fields.name: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (malignant lesion of the nose)
fields.definition: The predominant tumor type arising in the nasopharynx
fields.etiology: Associated with EBV (Epstein-Barr virus) and HPV (human papillomavirus)
fields.epidemiology: Rare in the US and Western Europe; endemic in Southern China (including Hong Kong), Southeast Asia, North Africa, the Middle East, and the Arctic; 2–3 times more common in males
fields.risk_factors: Smoking; high-salt diet; Chinese herbs; rancid butter and sheep fat (butyric acid)
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Headache, diplopia, facial numbness, neck mass
fields.diagnosis: ENT (ear, nose, and throat) referral; endoscopic-guided biopsy of the primary tumor
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Benign neoplasms of the nose
fields.definition: Same benign lesions as skin (see dermatology lectures): warts, freckles, hemangioma, port wine stain, among others
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

lectures.title: Neoplasms and Neck Masses
lectures.deck: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses - Shah Fallsv-2.pptx
lectures.note: Several conditions appear only as names in the KITTENS differential (slides 16-17) or the primary neoplasm table (slide 38) and are not taught: syphilis, sebaceous cyst, deep neck abscess, hematoma, thyroid hyperplasia, aberrant thyroid tissue, parathyroid cyst, salivary gland tumors, neurogenic tumors, lipoma, sarcomas, Ludwig angina, sialadenitis, melanoma. Thyroid staging (slide 43): the notes say it need not be memorized.

fields.name: Branchial cleft cyst (spelled "brachial" on slide 16 and in the slide 22 notes)
fields.definition: Congenital lateral neck cyst at the anterior border of the SCM (sternocleidomastoid) muscle
fields.etiology: Failure of the pharyngobranchial ducts to obliterate during fetal development
fields.epidemiology: Presents in late childhood or early adulthood
fields.risk_factors: Becomes apparent when infected, usually after a URI (upper respiratory infection)
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Tender, inflammatory mass at the anterior border of the SCM (sternocleidomastoid) muscle; overlying erythema and swelling if infected
fields.diagnosis: Rule out HPV (human papillomavirus)-associated SCC (squamous cell carcinoma) before confirming a congenital mass, since it can present as a cystic neck mass in an adult
fields.treatment: Control infection first (antibiotics), then surgical excision of cyst and tract (definitive); avoid I&D (incision and drainage) unless acute abscess (needle aspiration/decompression preferred) because I&D makes definitive excision harder

fields.name: Thyroglossal duct cyst
fields.definition: Congenital midline mass of the anterior neck, intimately related to the hyoid bone
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: About one third of all congenital neck masses
fields.risk_factors: Often appears only when infected, usually after a URI (upper respiratory infection)
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Midline anterior neck mass, may be asymptomatic; location variable (can be lateral or as low as the thyroid gland), off-midline ones hard to tell from branchial cleft cyst; erythema and edema if infected
fields.diagnosis: Pathognomonic sign: vertical motion of the mass with swallowing or tongue protrusion (shows its attachment to the hyoid bone); histopathology of every excised cyst to rule out thyroid carcinoma
fields.treatment: Antibiotics if infected; Sistrunk operation (standard; cyst excised with a cuff of tissue including the center of the hyoid bone), avoiding injury to the hypoglossal nerves

fields.name: Laryngocele (external laryngocele); infected form: laryngopyocele
fields.definition: Abnormal dilation or herniation of the saccule of the larynx
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Dilated/herniated laryngeal saccule; secondary infection produces a laryngopyocele
fields.clinical: Cough, hoarseness, dyspnea, dysphagia, foreign body sensation, or any combination
fields.diagnosis: Laryngoscopy (smooth dilation at the level of the false cord); CT (computed tomography) confirms the diagnosis and details the extent
fields.treatment: Treat if symptomatic: laryngoscopic decompression (small), external surgical excision (large; protect the superior laryngeal nerve), or laser endoscopy

fields.name: Plunging ranula
fields.definition: Mucocele or retention cyst of the floor of the mouth, called plunging when it extends through the mylohyoid muscle into the neck
fields.etiology: Arises from the sublingual gland
fields.pathology: Sublingual gland mucocele/retention cyst extending through the mylohyoid muscle into the neck
fields.clinical: Slow-growing, painless submental mass
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Excision of the sublingual gland

fields.name: Lymphangioma
fields.definition: Congenital malformation of the lymphatic channels
fields.etiology: Failure of the lymph spaces to connect to the rest of the lymphatic system
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Soft, doughy, smooth, nontender, compressible mass; positive transillumination ("positive illumination" on the slide)
fields.diagnosis: CT (computed tomography) and MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) to confirm extent and define associated abnormalities such as hemangiomas
fields.treatment: Surgical excision vs debulking (removing as much as possible) depending on infiltration; sclerotherapy (injected agent shrinks the vessels over time)

fields.name: Hemangioma
fields.definition: Malformation of vascular tissue
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Presents in the first few months of life
fields.pathology: Grows rapidly during the first year, then slowly involutes from 18 to 24 months of age
fields.clinical: Red or bluish soft, compressible mass that enlarges with straining or crying; with or without bruits
fields.diagnosis: CT (computed tomography), MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)
fields.treatment: Observation alone for most; intervene for airway compromise, skin ulceration, dysphagia, thrombocytopenia, or cardiac failure: first line propranolol (if no contraindication); second line systemic corticosteroids, interferon alpha, surgical laser excision

fields.name: Teratoma
fields.definition: Rare germ cell tumor that may contain immature or fully formed tissue (including hair, teeth, muscle)
fields.etiology: Originates from pluripotent cells
fields.epidemiology: Head and neck teratomas are 3.5% of all teratomas; most noted at birth or within the first year of life
fields.pathology: Pluripotent-cell tumor containing immature or fully formed tissues
fields.clinical: Firm neck mass; when large, respiratory compromise or dysphagia
fields.diagnosis: CT (computed tomography) and MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) show calcifications; caution with CT radiation in young children, who may need sedation
fields.treatment: Surgical excision

fields.name: Dermoid cyst
fields.definition: Congenital cyst from epithelium entrapped in deeper tissue
fields.etiology: Epithelium entrapped in deeper tissue during embryogenesis or by traumatic implantation
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Midline, nontender, mobile neck mass in the submental region
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Surgical excision (mainstay)

fields.name: Thymic cyst
fields.definition: Congenital neck mass (listed under Endocrine in the KITTENS differential)
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Slow-growing, asymptomatic mass; may be painful if infected
fields.diagnosis: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) and CT (computed tomography) useful for the differential; definitive diagnosis by biopsy (Hassall corpuscles present)
fields.treatment: Surgical excision

fields.name: Sternocleidomastoid (SCM) tumor of infancy
fields.definition: Benign mass within the SCM (sternocleidomastoid) muscle in infants, related to congenital torticollis (head turned to one side by the neck muscles)
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Slowly enlarges for 2-3 months, then regresses over 4-8 months
fields.clinical: Firm, painless, discrete mass within the SCM (sternocleidomastoid) muscle
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Physical therapy to prevent restrictive torticollis; surgical excision only for persistent cases

fields.name: Reactive viral lymphadenopathy (viral lymphadenitis)
fields.definition: Reactive cervical lymph node enlargement with a viral URI (upper respiratory infection)
fields.etiology: Adenovirus, rhinovirus, enterovirus (most common); associated with an underlying URI
fields.epidemiology: Most common cause of cervical lymphadenopathy in children
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Cervical lymphadenopathy with URI (upper respiratory infection) symptoms
fields.diagnosis: A node larger than 1 cm is abnormal and needs further workup (biopsy for fungal, granulomatous, neoplastic causes) if it persists more than 4-6 weeks or enlarges
fields.treatment: Observation

fields.name: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) / mononucleosis lymphadenopathy
fields.definition: Cervical lymphadenopathy caused by EBV (Epstein-Barr virus) mononucleosis
fields.etiology: EBV (Epstein-Barr virus)
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Lymphadenopathy with tonsil and adenoid enlargement, fever, pharyngitis; palpate liver and spleen
fields.diagnosis: EBV (Epstein-Barr virus) monospot
fields.treatment: Supportive

fields.name: HIV (human immunodeficiency virus)-associated cervical adenopathy
fields.definition: Cervical lymph node enlargement in patients with HIV (human immunodeficiency virus)
fields.etiology: Idiopathic follicular hyperplasia is the most common cause
fields.epidemiology: Present in 12%-45% of patients with HIV
fields.pathology: Idiopathic follicular hyperplasia (most common)
fields.clinical: Cervical adenopathy
fields.diagnosis: Rule out Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Pneumocystis carinii, lymphoma, Kaposi sarcoma; HIV testing among neck mass labs
fields.treatment: Treat the HIV

fields.name: Persistent generalized lymphadenopathy
fields.definition: Lymphadenopathy without an identifiable infectious or neoplastic cause
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Commonly seen in patients with HIV (human immunodeficiency virus)
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Generalized lymphadenopathy; the neck is the most common site
fields.diagnosis: Diagnosis made when no infectious or neoplastic cause can be determined
fields.treatment: Treat the HIV (human immunodeficiency virus)

fields.name: Suppurative (bacterial) lymphadenopathy
fields.definition: Bacterial infection of cervical lymph nodes
fields.etiology: Most commonly Staphylococcus aureus and group A B-Streptococcus (as written on the slide)
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Neck mass usually in the submandibular or jugulodigastric region, with sore throat, skin lesions, URI (upper respiratory infection) symptoms
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Empirical antibiotics against anaerobic and gram-positive organisms; FNA (fine needle aspiration) or I&D (incision and drainage) if antibiotics fail

fields.name: Toxoplasmosis
fields.definition: Infectious cause of neck lymphadenopathy due to Toxoplasma gondii
fields.etiology: Toxoplasma gondii; contracted through poorly cooked meat or ingestion of "oocytes" (as written on the slide) in cat feces
fields.risk_factors: Poorly cooked meat; exposure to cat feces
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Fever, malaise, sore throat, myalgias
fields.diagnosis: Serologic testing (immunoglobulin; toxoplasmosis titers)
fields.treatment: Sulfonamides or pyrimethamine

fields.name: Tularemia
fields.definition: Infectious cause of neck lymphadenopathy due to Francisella tularensis
fields.etiology: Francisella tularensis; transmitted by rabbits, ticks, contaminated water
fields.risk_factors: Exposure to rabbits, ticks, contaminated water
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Tonsillitis, painful adenopathy, fever, chills, headache, fatigue
fields.diagnosis: Serologic testing and cultures
fields.treatment: Streptomycin

fields.name: Brucellosis
fields.definition: Infectious cause of lymphadenopathy due to Brucella
fields.etiology: Brucella; transmitted by ingestion of unpasteurized milk
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Total body lymphadenopathy, fever, fatigue, malaise
fields.diagnosis: Serology and cultures
fields.treatment: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or tetracycline

fields.name: Cat scratch disease (cat-scratch fever)
fields.definition: Granulomatous infection causing neck lymphadenopathy after cat contact
fields.etiology: Bartonella henselae
fields.epidemiology: Common in patients younger than 20 years
fields.pathology: Granulomatous disease (specific tissue pattern on biopsy from cell injury)
fields.clinical: Lymphadenopathy (commonly preauricular and submandibular), fever, malaise
fields.diagnosis: Serologic testing with indirect fluorescent antibodies; cat scratch antigen titers
fields.treatment: Self-limiting vs azithromycin

fields.name: Actinomycosis
fields.definition: Granulomatous infection presenting as a neck mass
fields.etiology: Actinomyces
fields.pathology: Granulomatous disease (specific tissue pattern on biopsy from cell injury)
fields.clinical: Painless, fluctuant neck mass in the submandibular or upper digastric region
fields.diagnosis: Clinical and biopsy
fields.treatment: Penicillin

fields.name: Atypical mycobacteria (atypical mycobacterial infection)
fields.definition: Granulomatous mycobacterial infection of the neck in children
fields.etiology: Atypical mycobacteria
fields.pathology: Granulomatous disease (specific tissue pattern on biopsy from cell injury)
fields.clinical: Unilateral neck mass in the anterior triangle or parotid gland; brawny (reddish-brown) skin, induration, pain
fields.diagnosis: Stain or culture for acid-fast bacilli; skin testing
fields.treatment: Surgical excision vs I&D (incision and drainage) plus antibiotics

fields.name: Tuberculosis (TB) of the neck; cervical TB is called scrofula
fields.definition: Cervical lymphadenitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis
fields.etiology: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
fields.pathology: Granulomatous disease (specific tissue pattern on biopsy from cell injury)
fields.clinical: Lymphadenopathy more diffuse and bilateral than atypical mycobacteria
fields.diagnosis: TB (tuberculosis) skin test (PPD, purified protein derivative; notes contrast QuantiFERON gold); stain and culture for acid-fast bacilli
fields.treatment: Isoniazid, rifampin, rifabutin, rifapentine, pyrazinamide, ethambutol; traditionally RIPE (rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol)

fields.name: Fungal infection (of the neck)
fields.definition: Fungal infectious inflammatory neck disorder
fields.etiology: Most common organisms: Candida, Histoplasma, Aspergillus
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Fungal cultures and serology required
fields.treatment: Amphotericin B; treat aggressively and early

fields.name: Noninfectious inflammatory disorders (e.g., Sjogren syndrome, sarcoidosis, IgG4 (immunoglobulin G4)-related sialadenitis, Kawasaki disease)
fields.definition: Inflammatory neck masses without an infectious cause
fields.etiology: Generally autoimmune
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Many patients have specific symptoms that point to the underlying disorder
fields.diagnosis: ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate), CRP (C-reactive protein), autoimmune panel
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Neck neoplasm / neoplastic neck mass
fields.definition: Benign tumors arise from neck soft tissue (fat, salivary tissue, lymph nodes, blood vessels, nerves); malignant tumors represent metastatic disease
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Neck masses under 40 are mostly inflammatory (exception: Hodgkin lymphoma); high risk of malignancy in adults
fields.risk_factors: Age over 40; tobacco and alcohol use; family or previous history of cancer; previous skin/scalp lesion excision; radiation; immunocompromise/HIV (human immunodeficiency virus)
fields.pathology: Malignant: sarcomas, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors, lymphoma, metastasis (mucosal head and neck, salivary, skin); benign: paragangliomas, arteriovenous malformations, schwannomas, neurofibromas, neuromas, lipomas
fields.clinical: Hoarseness, dysphagia, odynophagia; asymptomatic, slowly progressive, firm; malignant clues: no infectious origin, over 2 weeks, over 1.5 cm, firm, noncystic, nontender, little mobility, ulceration
fields.diagnosis: Presume malignant until proven otherwise; complete head and neck exam; fiberoptic laryngoscopy for occult primary; US (ultrasound), CT (computed tomography) with contrast, MRI (magnetic resonance imaging), PET (positron emission tomography); FNA (fine needle aspiration) biopsy
fields.treatment: Refer to specialists early if suspicious or persisting after treatment; early and aggressive treatment needed in some neoplastic conditions

conditions.name: Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma to the neck

fields.name: Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the neck
fields.definition: Most common metastatic lesion to the neck; malignant neck tumors mostly represent metastatic SCC from skin or upper aerodigestive tract
fields.etiology: Spread from SCC (squamous cell carcinoma) of the skin or upper aerodigestive tract (head and neck primary); HPV (human papillomavirus)-associated SCC
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic, slowly progressive, firm neck mass; HPV (human papillomavirus)-associated SCC may present as a cystic neck mass in an adult
fields.diagnosis: FNA (fine needle aspiration) biopsy, not excisional (avoids spillage and complicated definitive treatment); then examine all head and neck mucosa, thyroid, salivary glands, skin (usually finds the primary in office); panendoscopy-guided biopsy with possible tonsillectomy; CT (computed tomography), MRI (magnetic resonance imaging), PET (positron emission tomography)
fields.treatment: Primary found: treat primary tumor and neck; no primary found: radiation and neck dissection

fields.name: Paraganglioma (carotid body, vagal, jugulotympanic)
fields.definition: Benign vascular neoplasm of the neck
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Benign vascular neoplasm; types: carotid body, vagal, jugulotympanic
fields.clinical: Pulsatile neck mass (pulsatile or bruit means vascular)
fields.diagnosis: CT (computed tomography), MRI (magnetic resonance imaging), or MRA (magnetic resonance angiography) angiogram confirms; CTA (computed tomography angiography) for pulsatile masses
fields.treatment: Excise tumor or XRT (radiation therapy)

conditions.name: Lymphoma presenting as a neck mass

fields.name: Lymphoma (cervical nodal)
fields.definition: Primary neoplastic cause of a neck mass
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Hodgkin lymphoma is the exception to inflammatory masses in patients under 40
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Rapidly growing mass without infectious symptoms; check liver and spleen
fields.diagnosis: FNA (fine needle aspiration) separates carcinoma from lymphoma; node biopsy with staging
fields.treatment: Chemotherapy and XRT (radiation therapy)

fields.name: Thyroid mass / thyroid nodule
fields.definition: Thyroid nodule or mass; the main cause of anterior neck masses
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Main cause of anterior neck masses and lumps
fields.risk_factors: Age (adults under 30 or over 60); childhood head and neck irradiation; full-body irradiation for bone marrow transplant; family history of thyroid cancer; MEN-2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2)
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Immobile midline neck mass that elevates with swallowing; recent growth, dysphagia, obstruction; incidental nodules over 1 cm on imaging need evaluation
