fields.diagnosis: US (ultrasound) with FNA (fine needle aspiration), TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), T3/T4; FNA is the procedure of choice after labs; low TSH: technetium radionuclide scan first, hot (hyperfunctioning) needs no FNA, cold/warm needs FNA; avoid iodine CT contrast if cancer suspected
fields.treatment: Hot nodule: treat hyperthyroidism; FNA benign: follow; malignant: surgery; indeterminate: consider molecular testing and surgery; inadequate: repeat FNA, then surgery if still inadequate and suspicious
fields.mortality: Prognosis: hot (hyperfunctioning) nodule: low risk for malignancy

fields.name: Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC)
fields.definition: Most common thyroid cancer (75%)
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: 75% of thyroid cancers; most common in young females
fields.pathology: Involves thyroid epithelial cells
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: FNA (fine needle aspiration); staging differs by age: 45 or younger, stage I in thyroid or local nodes and stage II distant spread; 45 or older, stages I-IVC by size and spread
fields.treatment: Lobectomy vs thyroidectomy, with or without neck dissection, with or without ablation, and surveillance
fields.mortality: Prognosis: best prognosis of the thyroid cancers

fields.name: Follicular thyroid carcinoma (FTC); Hurthle cell variant
fields.definition: Second most common thyroid cancer (16%)
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Involves thyroid epithelial cells; spreads to local lymph nodes or by blood to bone and lungs
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: FNA (fine needle aspiration); staged with papillary cancer (age 45 cutoff, stages I-IVC by size and spread)
fields.treatment: Lobectomy vs thyroidectomy, with or without neck dissection, with or without ablation, and surveillance
fields.mortality: Prognosis: hurthle cell variant is more aggressive, with higher risk of metastases and recurrence

fields.name: Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC)
fields.definition: Thyroid cancer of the parafollicular (C) cells, about 5%
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.risk_factors: MEN-2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2) is listed as a thyroid-mass risk factor; family members of medullary patients are screened for MEN
fields.pathology: Disorder of parafollicular or C cells (produce calcitonin); insidious, most likely to metastasize
fields.clinical: Insidious; may go undiagnosed until a metastasis is found
fields.diagnosis: FNA (fine needle aspiration); own staging table, stages I-IVC (stage I: only in thyroid, 2 cm or smaller)
fields.treatment: Thyroidectomy and monitoring for recurrence (screening labs), with or without external beam radiation for nodal disease; screen family members for MEN (multiple endocrine neoplasia)
fields.mortality: Prognosis: most likely thyroid cancer to metastasize

fields.name: Anaplastic (undifferentiated) thyroid carcinoma
fields.definition: Most aggressive thyroid cancer, about 1%
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: 1% of thyroid cancers; commonly elderly patients
fields.pathology: Small cell, giant cell, spindle cell carcinoma; aggressive growth, often found after it has spread
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Staged only IVA-IVC (IVA in thyroid; IVB just outside thyroid; IVC distant, e.g., lungs)
fields.treatment: Resistant to all treatment modalities; slide 44 lists anaplastic with the exceptions to thyroidectomy ("needs an isthmectomy")

fields.name: Primary lymphoma of the thyroid
fields.definition: Lymphoma arising in the thyroid, most commonly non-Hodgkin B cell tumors
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Most commonly non-Hodgkin B cell tumor
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Hard to distinguish from Hashimoto thyroiditis by FNA (fine needle aspiration) alone; biopsy to confirm plus lymphoma staging
fields.treatment: Chemotherapy and radiation

lectures.title: Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands and Neck
lectures.deck: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands - Shah Fall UPDATEDsv.pptx

fields.name: Leukoedema (normal variant of the oral mucosa)
fields.definition: Common, benign mucosal change; a normal variant
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Accumulation of fluid within the epithelial cells of the buccal mucosa
fields.clinical: Asymptomatic, bilateral, grayish-white, semitransparent mucosal alteration that typically disappears when the mucosa is stretched
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Fordyce granules (Fordyce spots)
fields.definition: Normal variant: ectopic sebaceous glands (normal tissue cells in an abnormal location)
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Found in about 90% of the adult population
fields.pathology: Ectopic sebaceous glands in the oral mucosa
fields.clinical: White to yellow, 1-2 mm discrete papules, symmetrically distributed on the buccal mucosa and vermilion border of the lips
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Physiologic oral pigmentation
fields.definition: Normal variant of the oral mucosa with brown-gray pigmentation
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: Commonly seen in individuals with darker skin types
fields.pathology: Increased melanocyte activity and melanin production
fields.clinical: Typically bilateral brown-gray band on the gingiva; patches may be seen on the tongue, floor of mouth and buccal mucosa
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Stomatitis
fields.definition: Inflammation of the mouth and lips; any inflammatory process of the oral and lip mucous membranes, with or without ulceration
fields.etiology: Trauma (ill-fitting dentures or braces, biting cheek/tongue/lips), surgery, chemotherapy/radiation, viral infection (herpes, coxsackievirus), candidiasis, xerostomia (dry mouth), smoking/chewing tobacco, zinc or iron deficiency, allergic reactions, idiopathic (aphthous ulcers)
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Aphthous stomatitis (canker sores); recurrent form = Sutton disease
fields.definition: Painful oral ulcers on freely moving, nonkeratinized mucosa; recurrent aphthous stomatitis is called Sutton disease
fields.etiology: Cause unknown; human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) has been suggested
fields.epidemiology: Most common cause of acute recurrent oral ulcers in adolescents and young adults
fields.risk_factors: Trauma to the oral mucosa (cheek biting, dental procedures) exacerbates; stress predisposes
fields.pathology: Found on freely moving, nonkeratinized mucosa (buccal and labial mucosa, nonattached gingiva, palate); minor (<1 cm), major (>1 cm, multiple, scarring) and herpetiform (numerous 1-3 mm ulcers, scarring) forms
fields.clinical: Painful round ulcers with yellow-gray fibrinoid centers and red halos; minor: burning/tingling before ulcer, lasts 7-10 days; major and herpetiform: last over 1 month
fields.diagnosis: Clinical
fields.treatment: Observation (self-limiting); consider anti-inflammatories, antibiotics, antivirals, oral/topical corticosteroids (triamcinolone, fluocinonide), silver nitrate cauterization, Lactobacillus capsules, Kanka, dilute water rinses
fields.mortality: Prognosis: self-limiting disorder; major and herpetiform ulcers carry a risk of scarring

fields.name: Behcet syndrome
fields.definition: Inflammatory multisystem disorder with vascular, articular, gastrointestinal, neurologic, urogenital, pulmonary and cardiac involvement
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Oral ulcers are the most common feature (up to 100% of patients); genital ulcers in about 75%, resembling oral aphthae
fields.diagnosis: Clinical: recurrent aphthous ulcers plus characteristic systemic manifestations
fields.treatment: No cure; corticosteroids, IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin), immunosuppressants (colchicine, azathioprine, cyclosporine, interferon alfa, cyclophosphamide)

fields.name: Oral lichen planus; types: reticular, plaque, atrophic, erosive/bullous, ulcerative, annular
fields.definition: Common chronic inflammatory autoimmune disorder in which activated lymphocytes destroy the basal layer
fields.etiology: May be familial or medication-induced (penicillamine, methyldopa, phenothiazines, antimalarials)
fields.pathology: Activated lymphocytes destroy the epithelial basal layer; Koebner (isomorphic) phenomenon (new lesions provoked by physical trauma such as scratching)
fields.clinical: Recurrent purple, polygonal, pruritic papules on flexor surfaces and trunk; 60-70% involve lips, oral mucosa, eyelids; Wickham striae (lacy white lines) on buccal mucosa in reticular type; erosive/ulcerative types painful
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Aimed at pain relief; remove reversible factors (medications, dental restorations, improve oral hygiene, avoid tobacco/alcohol); topical or oral corticosteroids; lidocaine, tacrolimus, cyclosporine; close follow-up
fields.mortality: Prognosis: 1-4% progress to squamous cell carcinoma, higher risk with ulcerative lesions

fields.name: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), oral involvement
fields.definition: Mucous membrane (oral) involvement in SLE (systemic lupus erythematosus)
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: 40% of patients with SLE (systemic lupus erythematosus) have mucous membrane involvement
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Oral lesions may be the first sign; painful or painless; no correlation with systemic activity; cheilitis, erythematous and honeycomb patches, white plaques, discoid and punched-out ulcers with surrounding erythema on lips, soft and buccal mucosa
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Photoprotection; topical or intralesional corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors, systemic glucocorticoids; systemic antimalarials (hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine)

fields.name: Herpes simplex ulcers; herpetic gingivostomatitis (primary)
fields.definition: Oral/perioral ulcers caused by HSV (herpes simplex virus) type 1 and 2
fields.etiology: HSV-1 and HSV-2 (herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2)
fields.epidemiology: Primary infection most common in seronegative children; herpetic gingivostomatitis is the most common primary manifestation in children and young adults
fields.risk_factors: Recurrence triggered by stress, trauma (including dental treatment), immunosuppression, ultraviolet light/sunlight, menstruation
fields.pathology: Secondary disease is reactivation of virus dormant in the trigeminal ganglion, migrating along the axonal sheath
fields.clinical: Prodrome of burning, tingling, pain about 24 hours before; small painful lesions ulcerate to an erythematous base with gray cover; odynophagia, fever, malaise, cervical lymphadenopathy; heals without scar in 1-2 weeks
fields.diagnosis: Clinical when characteristic lesions present; confirm with HSV DNA PCR (polymerase chain reaction; most sensitive and specific); IgG (immunoglobulin G)/IgM (immunoglobulin M) serology distinguishes HSV-1 from HSV-2; viral culture is definitive; Tzanck smear (multinucleated giant cells, also seen with varicella zoster)
fields.treatment: Oral acyclovir for treatment and prophylaxis
fields.mortality: Prognosis: resolves in 1-2 weeks, heals without a scar

fields.name: Acute suppurative sialadenitis
fields.definition: Bacterial infection of the salivary glands
fields.etiology: Staphylococcus aureus (most common), then Streptococcus viridans, Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pyogenes, Escherichia coli; Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Pseudomonas, Candida in chronically ill hospitalized patients
fields.epidemiology: Postoperative patients, elderly patients with chronic medical conditions, children younger than 2 months
fields.risk_factors: Dehydration, trauma, immunosuppression, debilitation, chemotherapy/radiation, age over 50, HIV (human immunodeficiency virus), xerostomia, sialolithiasis, anorexia/bulimia
fields.pathology: Salivary stasis from duct stricture/obstruction reduces antibacterial activity; bacteria thought to ascend the parotid duct then spread hematogenously
fields.clinical: Usually unilateral parotid swelling (parotid most affected), firm and diffusely tender; overlying erythema; trismus, purulent ductal discharge (can be massaged from the duct), induration, fever, chills
fields.diagnosis: Usually clinical; if uncertain: culture (fine-needle aspiration not required), ultrasound, CT (computed tomography) or MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) to check for stones, abscess, gland inflammation
fields.treatment: Rehydration; IV (intravenous) penicillinase-resistant gram-positive coverage (nafcillin or cefazolin) then oral dicloxacillin or clindamycin; warm compresses, massage, sialogogues (lemon drops, vitamin C lozenges), oral hygiene; no improvement in 48 hours suggests abscess: incision and drainage or image-guided aspiration
fields.mortality: Most respond to medical therapy; mortality is higher with coexisting medical conditions; can progress to abscess

fields.name: Chronic granulomatous sialadenitis
fields.definition: Chronic unilateral or bilateral salivary gland swelling with minimal pain
fields.etiology: Consider primary tuberculosis if risk factors present; differential includes cat scratch disease, sarcoidosis, actinomycosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener granulomatosis), syphilis
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Chronic unilateral or bilateral salivary gland swelling with minimal pain
fields.diagnosis: Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the gland
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Sialolithiasis (salivary calculi, salivary stones)
fields.definition: Salivary gland stones causing obstruction
fields.etiology: Change in saliva viscosity, ductal epithelial injury, salivary stagnation (dehydration) cause calcium phosphate/carbonate precipitation
fields.epidemiology: 80-90% submandibular gland, 10-20% parotid, very few sublingual/minor glands; more common in men
fields.risk_factors: Long illnesses with dehydration, gout, diabetes, hypertension
fields.pathology: Submandibular predominance from longer duct, more mucin, alkaline saliva, high calcium/phosphate; submandibular stones are calcium phosphate and hydroxyapatite and radiopaque
fields.clinical: Recurrent submandibular swelling and pain worse with eating (salivary colic); infection with prolonged obstruction; xerostomia; gritty sand-like particles in mouth; stone palpable in anterior two thirds of submandibular duct
fields.diagnosis: Usually clinical; confirm with x-ray, ultrasound (echogenic structure with acoustic shadow), CT (most sensitive), digital subtraction sialography (most accurate)
fields.treatment: Conservative: hydration, hot compresses, gland massage, NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), lozenges; removal by size/location: intraoral extraction (anterior duct), sialoendoscopy +/- open sialolithotomy, gland excision for hilum/body stones, interventional radiology, lithotripsy

fields.name: Parotitis
fields.definition: Painful swelling of the parotid gland
fields.etiology: Viral: mumps (paramyxovirus), herpes, Epstein-Barr virus; other: bacterial infection, diabetes, tumors, stones, dental problems
fields.pathology: Swelling or inflammation of the parotid gland in response to the cause
fields.clinical: Painful swelling of the parotid gland
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Vocal cord nodules; screamer's nodules (children); singer's nodules
fields.definition: Smooth, paired lesions at the junction of the anterior one third and posterior two thirds of the vocal folds
fields.etiology: Vocal abuse
fields.epidemiology: Most common cause of persistent dysphonia in children; frequent cause of voice deterioration in professional singers
fields.pathology: Paired lesions at the junction of the anterior one third and posterior two thirds of the vocal folds
fields.clinical: Hoarseness; persistent dysphonia
fields.diagnosis: Laryngoscopy: small, well-defined, whitish, bilateral and symmetric vocal cord lesions
fields.treatment: Speech therapy is first line in adults and children (photodocumentation tracks progress); microlaryngoscopy

fields.name: Vocal cord polyps
fields.definition: Unilateral fluid-filled masses of gelatinous material within the superficial lamina propria of the vocal fold
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Pedunculated, unilateral, fluid-filled gelatinous lesions in the superficial lamina propria at the point of maximal vibration (junction of anterior and middle thirds); may show vascular markings
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Microlaryngoscopic examination with excision confirms diagnosis and excludes other pathology; a large polyp may conceal an early laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma
fields.treatment: Microlaryngoscopic excision; vocal rest and smoking cessation

fields.name: Vocal cord papillomatosis; recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP)
fields.definition: Benign, noncontagious, rare condition with exophytic warty lesions, usually in the larynx (also nose, pharynx, trachea)
fields.etiology: HPV (human papillomavirus) subtypes 6 and 11, rarely 16
fields.epidemiology: Bimodal: juvenile at 2-4 years; adult peak in the 30s
fields.pathology: Multiple friable irregular warty growths on true and false cords, at areas of airway constriction with turbulence, mucosal drying/cooling, and ciliary-to-squamous epithelial junctions
fields.clinical: Glottic lesions: dysphonia; supraglottic: stridor; hoarseness, airway obstruction; less often chronic cough, pneumonia, failure to thrive, dyspnea
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: No cure for HPV (human papillomavirus); remove symptomatic lesions (carbon dioxide laser, cold steel dissection, microdebrider); avoid tracheostomy (new squamociliary junction); adjuvant intralesional cidofovir (off-label); HPV vaccine (Gardasil, Gardasil 9) may prevent
fields.mortality: Prognosis: spontaneous remission occurs but recurrence may come years later; 3-7% risk of malignancy

fields.name: Vocal cord paralysis
fields.definition: Voice disorder in which one or both vocal folds do not open or close properly
fields.etiology: Surgical injury (thyroid/parathyroid, esophagus, neck, chest), neck/chest trauma, tumors, infections (Lyme disease, Epstein-Barr virus, herpes, possibly COVID-19), neurologic (stroke, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson disease)
fields.pathology: Recurrent laryngeal nerve or vagus nerve injury; unilateral or bilateral
fields.clinical: Unilateral: hoarse breathy dysphonia, aspiration, dysphagia, short phonation time, vocal fatigue, stridor in children, or asymptomatic; bilateral: inspiratory or biphasic stridor, weak cry, aspiration, hoarseness
fields.diagnosis: Mirror laryngoscopy or flexible nasolaryngoscopy; full neurologic exam; laryngeal electromyography for prognosis
fields.treatment: Determine if self-limiting or permanent; observation with voice therapy; surgical medialization of the affected fold (implant), thyroplasty
fields.mortality: Prognosis: transected nerve or malignant infiltration will not recover; bruised or stretched nerve may recover in 6 months to 1 year

fields.name: Acute laryngitis
fields.definition: Most common cause of hoarseness; persists about a week after upper respiratory infection symptoms clear
fields.etiology: Viral (rhinovirus most common; parainfluenza, respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, influenza, pertussis), bacterial, fungal, acid reflux, smoking, toxic inhalation, cough, vocal abuse, direct injury, allergy
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Dysphonia, hoarseness, low-grade fever, cough, rhinitis, postnasal drip
fields.diagnosis: Clinical
fields.treatment: Conservative: hydration, antipyretics, voice rest, decongestants, humidification, smoking cessation; antibiotics only if secondary bacterial infection suspected

fields.name: Chronic laryngitis
fields.definition: Voice disturbance lasting more than 2 weeks; not a true diagnosis
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Voice disturbance lasting more than 2 weeks
fields.diagnosis: Always work up underlying cause (consider laryngeal cancer, vocal cord polyps); refer to ENT (ear, nose and throat) for laryngoscopy
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture

fields.name: Epiglottitis; supraglottitis (more correct term)
fields.definition: ENT (ear, nose and throat) emergency: cellulitis of multiple areas of the supraglottis
fields.etiology: Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b), most common in children; Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, beta-hemolytic Streptococcus
fields.epidemiology: Children 2-6 years, but any age including adults; rare; incidence down over 90% since Hib vaccine
fields.pathology: Cellulitis of the supraglottis with edema and erythema
fields.clinical: Children, sudden rapid onset, 4 Ds: drooling, dysphagia, dysphonia (hot potato voice), distress; tripod position (sitting, leaning forward) with sniffing position (neck hyperextended, chin thrust forward); adults, slower: severe sore throat, odynophagia, fever, dyspnea; inspiratory stridor is late
fields.diagnosis: Avoid anxiety-provoking exams (can obstruct airway); lateral neck x-ray thumbprint sign (swollen epiglottis), not needed for diagnosis; CT (computed tomography) similar; laryngoscopy is gold standard
fields.treatment: Airway first; children: operating room (rigid bronchoscopy, emergency tracheotomy), inhalation anesthesia to inspect and confirm, endotracheal intubation, cultures, parenteral antibiotics; adults: observe, intubation/tracheostomy if obstructed, humidification, glucocorticoids, IV (intravenous) antibiotics, nebulized epinephrine; ceftriaxone/cefotaxime + vancomycin (allergy: vancomycin + quinolone or carbapenem); consult ID (infectious disease specialist)
fields.mortality: High mortality if not diagnosed and treated promptly; responds rapidly to treatment, extubation often possible in 48-72 hours

fields.name: Viral pharyngitis (tonsillitis if tonsils affected; pharyngotonsillitis if both)
fields.definition: Viral infection causing inflammation of the throat (pharyngitis) and/or tonsils (tonsillitis)
fields.etiology: Viral causes are 70% of pharyngitis: adenovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, herpes simplex virus, HIV (human immunodeficiency virus), influenza, parainfluenza, rhinovirus, coronavirus, echovirus, enteroviruses, coxsackievirus
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Sore throat, earache/headache, cough, rhinitis, laryngitis, hoarseness, fever, conjunctivitis, lymphadenopathy, herpangina (ulcerative vesicles over the tonsils)
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; no further testing
fields.treatment: Supportive: hydration, antipyretics, pain relievers

fields.name: Bacterial pharyngitis; strep throat; GABHS (group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus) pharyngitis
fields.definition: Bacterial infection of the pharynx/tonsils, most commonly GABHS (group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus)
fields.etiology: Bacteria are 30% of pharyngitis; most common GABHS; others group C/G streptococci, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Corynebacterium diphtheriae
fields.epidemiology: Children and adolescents (not younger than 3); peaks in winter and spring; droplet spread; incubation 2-5 days
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Fever over 100.4 F, sore throat, cervical lymphadenopathy, dysphagia, odynophagia, no cough, abdominal pain; tonsillar/pharyngeal erythema with purulent exudate
fields.diagnosis: Rapid antigen test; confirm a negative with throat culture; ASO (antistreptolysin O) titer called definitive (carriers); Centor criteria: fever, exudate, tender anterior nodes, no cough, age 3-14 (+1), 45 or older (-1)
fields.treatment: Supportive care; penicillin VK for 10 days or amoxicillin; IM (intramuscular) penicillin G if compliance concern; mild allergy: cephalexin, cefadroxil; severe allergy: erythromycin, clarithromycin, clindamycin
fields.mortality: Complications: untreated GABHS (group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus) can lead to rheumatic fever (rare) and peritonsillar abscess

fields.name: Rheumatic fever
fields.definition: Rare sequela of untreated GABHS (group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus) pharyngitis; inflammatory disease of joints, heart, skin and nervous system
fields.etiology: Untreated GABHS (group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus) infection
fields.epidemiology: Peak ages 5-15; rare before 4 and after 40
fields.pathology: Cross-reactive antibodies to streptococcal infection affect the heart (endocarditis, myocarditis, pericarditis)
fields.clinical: Onset about 2-3 weeks after infection (range 1-5); JONES major: polyarthritis, carditis, nodules, erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea; minor: arthralgia, fever, prolonged PR interval, elevated ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate)/CRP (C-reactive protein)
fields.diagnosis: JONES criteria: 2 major, or 1 major and 2 minor, with evidence of recent group A strep infection
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture
fields.mortality: Prognosis: typically resolves after about 6 weeks

fields.name: Chronic pharyngitis
fields.definition: Persistent pharyngeal inflammation from ongoing irritants or underlying disease
fields.etiology: Postnasal drip (chronic rhinosinusitis), irritants (dust, dry heat, chemicals, smoking, alcohol), chronic mouth breathing, voice abuse, allergy, granulomatous disease, connective tissue disorder, malignancy
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Constant throat clearing, dry throat, odynophagia, thickened granular pharyngeal wall, pharyngeal crusting
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; culture and biopsy if therapy fails
fields.treatment: Address underlying disorder, avoid precipitating factors, symptomatic treatment

fields.name: Infectious mononucleosis (mono)
fields.definition: Highly contagious viral disease
fields.etiology: EBV (Epstein-Barr virus) 90%; CMV (cytomegalovirus) and other viruses 10%
fields.epidemiology: Ages 15-24; 90-95% of adults are EBV (Epstein-Barr virus) seropositive; spread by oral contact or infected saliva
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Prodrome of malaise, headache, low-grade fever (may be asymptomatic under age 10); triad: fever, tonsillar pharyngitis +/- exudate, cervical lymphadenopathy; palatal petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, rash in 5%; penicillin (for example, amoxicillin) can trigger a rash (exanthem)
fields.diagnosis: WBC (white blood cell count) with differential and heterophile (Monospot) test; positive confirms; negative suggests CMV (cytomegalovirus), confirm with EBV serology, IgM (immunoglobulin M) = current and IgG (immunoglobulin G) = past infection; PCR (polymerase chain reaction) for viral load in transplant
fields.treatment: Supportive (fluids, NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), acetaminophen, rest), no antiviral; corticosteroids for severe respiratory compromise; no heavy lifting/contact sports about 1 month until spleen normal on ultrasound
fields.mortality: Complication: splenic rupture risk with contact sports or heavy lifting while splenomegaly persists

fields.name: Oral candidiasis; thrush
fields.definition: Oral yeast infection
fields.etiology: Candida albicans; Aspergillus may also be cultured
fields.epidemiology: Common in infants and immunosuppressed patients such as HIV (human immunodeficiency virus)
fields.risk_factors: Dentures, debilitation with poor oral hygiene, diabetes mellitus, anemia, chemotherapy or local irradiation, oral or systemic corticosteroids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, elderly, HIV/immunocompromise
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Painful, granular, creamy white curd-like patches on an erythematous base on buccal mucosa and tongue that rub off (unlike leukoplakia or lichen planus); fever, lymphadenopathy, odynophagia, taste changes
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; KOH (potassium hydroxide) prep shows spores and pseudohyphae
fields.treatment: Saline and peroxide rinses; antifungals: nystatin oral suspension, clotrimazole, ketoconazole, fluconazole (longer in HIV); refractory: itraconazole or voriconazole

fields.name: Cervical adenitis (cervical lymphadenitis)
fields.definition: Inflammation of a cervical lymph node (often used as a synonym for lymphadenopathy, which is a sign, not a diagnosis)
fields.etiology: About 70% beta-hemolytic strep, 20% staphylococci including MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus), 10% viruses, atypical mycobacteria, Bartonella henselae (cat scratch fever); also toxoplasmosis, TB (tuberculosis), brucellosis, herpes simplex, syphilis, CMV (cytomegalovirus), HIV (human immunodeficiency virus), histoplasmosis, varicella; inflammatory, degenerative, neoplastic
fields.pathology: Local ear, nose and throat infections involve regional nodes and can form abscesses; nodes may stay palpable if scarred
fields.clinical: Typically a unilateral, solitary, anterior cervical node
fields.diagnosis: Response to antibiotics; describe size, shape, mobility (immobile suggests malignancy), consistency, tenderness (tender = inflammatory); FNA (fine-needle aspiration) biopsy if persistent or enlarging (possible lymphoma)
fields.treatment: Treat the underlying cause; incision and drainage if abscess

fields.name: Peritonsillar abscess; quinsy
fields.definition: Collection of pus between the palatine tonsil capsule and the pharyngeal muscles
fields.etiology: Complication of untreated strep throat or tonsillitis; aerobes: GABHS (group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus), Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae; anaerobes: Prevotella, Porphyromonas, Fusobacterium, Streptococcus
fields.epidemiology: Most common deep head and neck infection, especially young adults, adolescents and children; more common in males
fields.pathology: Pus collects between the tonsil capsule and pharyngeal muscles; edema pushes the soft palate and peritonsillar fold medially, deviating the uvula
fields.clinical: Severe sore throat, fever, odynophagia, dysphagia, hot potato voice; triad: trismus (inability to open jaw; most reliable), uvular deviation away from the involved side, dysphonia
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; confirmed by pus at drainage; CT (computed tomography) with contrast shows extent; ultrasound distinguishes abscess from cellulitis and guides aspiration
fields.treatment: Secure airway first; needle aspiration or incision and drainage; parenteral amoxicillin-clavulanate or clindamycin, adding MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) coverage if severe; oral if mild; tonsillectomy for recurrence, usually after infection resolves

fields.name: Retropharyngeal abscess
fields.definition: Abscess of the retropharyngeal space (skull base to posterior mediastinum)
fields.etiology: Spread from peritonsillar abscess or retropharyngeal node infection (adenitis to abscess); GABHS (group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus), Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, mixed flora
fields.epidemiology: More common in children under 5 after upper respiratory infection, otitis media, sinusitis; adults: intraoral procedures, trauma, foreign bodies (fishbone), immunocompromise, odontogenic spread
fields.risk_factors: Children: upper respiratory infection, otitis media, sinusitis; adults: intraoral procedures, trauma, foreign body, immunocompromise, dental infection
fields.pathology: Infection of retropharyngeal space nodes progresses to abscess; can spread into the danger and prevertebral spaces toward the mediastinum
fields.clinical: Early: fever, sore throat, pharyngeal erythema, dysphagia, odynophagia, neck stiffness, trismus; later: ill appearance, drooling, leaning forward with neck extended, respiratory distress
fields.diagnosis: Labs; lateral neck x-ray: widened retropharyngeal (prevertebral soft tissue) space; CT (gold standard): rim-enhancing hypodense collection; distinguish abscess from adenitis
fields.treatment: Surgical emergency; protect airway; antibiotics covering streptococci, anaerobes, S. aureus: ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin + ceftriaxone; vancomycin or linezolid if no improvement; then oral amoxicillin-clavulanate or clindamycin
fields.mortality: Complications: mediastinitis (50% mortality), respiratory distress, rupture with aspiration pneumonia, spread to danger and prevertebral spaces

fields.name: Ludwig angina
fields.definition: Emergency: severe infection (cellulitis) of the floor of mouth and submental, sublingual and submandibular spaces
fields.etiology: Streptococci, staphylococci, Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Klebsiella (usually in diabetes with other flora); offending tooth or teeth
fields.pathology: Posterior spread of cellulitis displaces tongue up and back; pus coalesces in the floor of mouth and can occlude the airway
fields.clinical: Edema and erythema of upper neck under the chin and floor of mouth; tongue displaced up and back; pus in floor of mouth
fields.diagnosis: CT (computed tomography) with contrast: separates inflammation/phlegmon from abscess and shows extent
fields.treatment: Antibiotics: penicillin + metronidazole, ampicillin-sulbactam, clindamycin, selected cephalosporins; external drainage via bilateral submental incision if airway threatened or medical therapy fails; dental consultation
fields.mortality: Complications: can rapidly compromise upper airway, requiring a surgical airway

fields.name: Diphtheria; nasal, laryngeal, pharyngeal (most common) and cutaneous forms
fields.definition: Acute Corynebacterium diphtheriae infection, usually of respiratory tract, also mucous membranes or skin wounds
fields.etiology: Corynebacterium diphtheriae, spread by respiratory secretions
fields.epidemiology: Common in nonimmunized children older than 6
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Pharyngeal: tenacious gray membrane over tonsils and pharynx, mild sore throat, fever, malaise, toxemia, prostration; nasal discharge; laryngeal airway obstruction; myocarditis (arrhythmia, heart block, heart failure); cranial neuropathy (diplopia, slurred speech, dysphagia)
fields.diagnosis: Clinical, confirmed by culture; differentiate from strep pharyngitis, mononucleosis, adenovirus, herpes simplex, candidiasis
fields.treatment: Laryngoscopy or bronchoscopy for airway; antitoxin from CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) to all; penicillin or erythromycin for 14 days; isolate until 3 negative cultures; treat contacts with erythromycin; prevent with childhood immunization, adult tetanus boosters, Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertussis vaccine) each pregnancy (27-36 weeks)

fields.name: Dental abscess; types: periapical, gingival, periodontal, pericoronal
fields.definition: Buildup of pus inside the teeth or gums
fields.etiology: Bacterial infection accumulated in the soft pulp of the tooth
fields.pathology: Periapical at root tip; gingival between gum and tooth; periodontal in periodontal pocket; pericoronal around impacted/partly erupted tooth
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Antibiotics (amoxicillin, ampicillin-sulbactam, amoxicillin-clavulanate, azithromycin, clindamycin, erythromycin, cephalexin, metronidazole, penicillin VK, ticarcillin-clavulanate); incision and drainage; root canal if restorable, else extraction with apical curettage

fields.name: Diseases of the gingiva: gingivitis (mildest) and periodontitis (periodontal/gum disease)
fields.definition: Gingivitis: plaque-driven gingival inflammation; periodontitis: untreated gingivitis with periodontal ligament/bone destruction and pockets
fields.etiology: Bacterial plaque, inadequate oral hygiene; gram-negative bacteria (A. actinomycetemcomitans, P. gingivalis, P. intermedia, B. forsythus, C. rectus, E. nodatum, P. micros, S. intermedius, Treponema)
fields.epidemiology: With dental caries, a primary cause of tooth loss
fields.risk_factors: Diabetes, smoking, aging, genetics, systemic disorders, stress, poor nutrition, puberty, hormone changes, pregnancy, substance abuse, HIV (human immunodeficiency virus), certain medications
fields.pathology: Plaque at gum line causes hyperemia (gingivitis); spreads below gum line, bacterial toxins drive chronic inflammation; gums separate, pockets deepen, ligament and bone destroyed, teeth loosen and fall out
fields.clinical: Gingivitis: erythematous, edematous gums that bleed easily with little to no discomfort; periodontitis: pockets, loosening and loss of teeth
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Gingivitis reversible with professional treatment and good home care; prevention: brushing, flossing, mouthwash, know your risk
fields.mortality: Associated conditions: heart disease/stroke (endocarditis risk), pneumonia, osteoporosis, kidney, pancreatic and blood cancers in men

conditions.name: Dental caries, pulpitis and periapical abscess

fields.name: Dental caries (cavities), pulpitis and periapical abscess
fields.definition: Pulpitis: inflammation of the tooth pulp; periapical abscess: pus pocket at the root of the tooth
fields.etiology: Tooth decay (most common), then injury
fields.epidemiology: Dental caries and periodontal disease are primary causes of tooth loss
fields.pathology: Mild inflammation may resolve without permanent pulp damage; severe inflammation may kill the pulp; infection forms a periapical abscess at the root
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Not covered in the lecture
fields.mortality: Complications: if untreated, infection may spread to the jaw or other sites (brain, sinus)

fields.name: Impacted teeth
fields.definition: Tooth unable to emerge because of insufficient room
fields.etiology: Overcrowding of teeth with insufficient room for the new tooth
fields.epidemiology: Wisdom teeth are usually impacted (last permanent teeth to erupt)
fields.pathology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.clinical: Not covered in the lecture
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Usually removed (little use in chewing)
fields.mortality: Complication: more likely to become infected

fields.name: Malocclusion
fields.definition: Abnormal alignment of the teeth and how upper and lower teeth fit together
fields.etiology: Jaw-tooth size mismatch, thumb sucking or tongue thrusting, lost teeth, birth defects
fields.pathology: Unequal distribution of chewing (about 150 lb) and clenching (about 250 lb) forces wears teeth, causing fractures and loosening
fields.clinical: Worn teeth, fractures, loose teeth
fields.diagnosis: Not covered in the lecture
fields.treatment: Braces, aligners, tooth removal, surgery

fields.name: Temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disorders; TMD (temporomandibular disorders); categories: myofascial pain, internal derangement, arthritis
fields.definition: Disorders of the TMJ (temporomandibular joint), masticatory muscles or both; second most common musculoskeletal cause of pain and disability
fields.etiology: Predisposing: trauma (blow to jaw, whiplash), stress (nocturnal bruxism); perpetuating: stress, poor coping, clenching/grinding, poor posture
fields.epidemiology: Common in women of childbearing age (possible sex hormone link)
fields.risk_factors: Trauma, stress, clenching/grinding, poor coping, poor posture
fields.pathology: Myofascial pain (jaw muscles), internal derangement (displaced disc, dislocation, condyle injury), arthritis (degenerative or inflammatory)
fields.clinical: Jaw/face/head pain; limited opening, catching, locking; clicking, popping, grating; headache, neck/shoulder pain; tinnitus, ear fullness, hearing loss, dizziness; abnormal tooth wear, sensitivity
fields.diagnosis: Clinical; CT (computed tomography)/MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) if abnormal pain or dysfunction not responding to short-term therapy; differentiate articular vs muscle disorders
fields.treatment: Self-care; NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), cyclobenzaprine, low-dose tricyclics (amitriptyline, desipramine, nortriptyline), oral methylprednisolone if synovitis; physical therapy, TENS (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation), acupuncture, mouth guards, arthrocentesis, arthroscopy, surgery
fields.mortality: Prognosis: not life threatening, but major impact on quality of life

fields.name: Oral leukoplakia
fields.definition: Premalignant white oral lesion that cannot be scraped off (unlike candidiasis) and cannot be attributed to another lesion
fields.etiology: Chronic irritation, smoking, infection
fields.risk_factors: Smoking and chewing tobacco, alcohol, chronic irritation
fields.pathology: Altered squamous epithelium with increased risk of SCC (squamous cell carcinoma)
fields.clinical: White lesion of the oral mucosa that cannot be scraped off
fields.diagnosis: Excisional biopsy to rule out malignancy
fields.treatment: Complete intraoral exam and node palpation; remove carcinogenic irritants (tobacco, alcohol); observation with serial biopsies and excisions
fields.mortality: Prognosis: 5-20% progress to SCC (squamous cell carcinoma)

fields.name: Erythroplakia
fields.definition: Premalignant lesion like leukoplakia but with an erythematous (red) component
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.pathology: 90% are dysplastic or carcinoma
fields.clinical: Leukoplakia-like lesion with a red component
fields.diagnosis: As for leukoplakia: excisional biopsy
fields.treatment: As for leukoplakia: remove irritants, observation with serial biopsies and excisions
fields.mortality: Prognosis: higher malignancy risk than leukoplakia (25%)

fields.name: Hairy leukoplakia
fields.definition: Benign mucosal hyperplasia
fields.etiology: EBV (Epstein-Barr virus); long-term systemic corticosteroids, solid organ transplant
fields.epidemiology: Strongly associated with HIV (human immunodeficiency virus); common early finding in HIV
fields.risk_factors: HIV, long-term systemic corticosteroids, solid organ transplant
fields.pathology: Benign mucosal hyperplasia
fields.clinical: Painless lateral tongue lesions that wax and wane
fields.diagnosis: Clinical and biopsy
fields.treatment: Observation; acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir give temporary resolution

fields.name: Benign salivary gland neoplasm; pleomorphic adenoma, basal cell adenoma
fields.definition: Benign tumor of the salivary glands; most parotid benign tumors are epithelial
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: 64-80% of salivary tumors are parotid (75-80% benign); submandibular 7-15% (50-60% benign); sublingual 1%; minor glands about 15% (35% benign)
fields.pathology: Parotid: mostly epithelial tumors; minor glands: pleomorphic adenoma most common, then basal cell adenoma
fields.clinical: Slow-growing painless mass, often at the tail of the parotid
fields.diagnosis: FNA (fine-needle aspiration), less accurate than for other tumors but helps separate benign from malignant; diffusion-weighted MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)/CT (computed tomography) for deep lobe tumors
fields.treatment: Complete surgical excision; no radiation
fields.mortality: Excellent prognosis and rare recurrence after removal; recurrence with positive margins; facial numbness or paralysis after surgery

fields.name: Malignant salivary gland neoplasm; mucoepidermoid carcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, adenocarcinoma
fields.definition: Malignant tumor of the salivary glands
fields.etiology: Not covered in the lecture
fields.epidemiology: 3-4% of head and neck malignancies and under 0.5% of all cancers; parotid most often affected
fields.pathology: Parotid: mucoepidermoid carcinoma most common; minor glands: adenoid cystic carcinoma and adenocarcinoma
fields.clinical: Painless mass
fields.diagnosis: FNA (fine-needle aspiration) helps separate malignant from benign but is less accurate than for other tumors; diffusion-weighted MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)/CT (computed tomography)
fields.treatment: Surgical removal; radiation for certain stages (T1 and T2); chemotherapy as palliation
fields.mortality: Poor prognosis with pain, facial or other nerve involvement, high-grade histology, skin/tissue invasion, recurrence

fields.name: Oral cavity and oropharyngeal neoplasm (cancer)
fields.definition: Cancer of the anterior two thirds of the tongue, buccal mucosa, floor of mouth, hard palate, gingiva, retromolar trigone (oral cavity), or posterior tongue, palatine tonsil, soft palate, posterior pharyngeal wall (oropharynx)
fields.etiology: Oropharyngeal: 60-80% from HPV (human papillomavirus); lip: 90% from chronic sun exposure
fields.epidemiology: Males 2-4 times (oral cavity) and 3-5 times (oropharynx) more than females; rises with age, mean 62
fields.risk_factors: Tobacco (chewing and smoking), alcohol, betel nut, poor oral hygiene, immunosuppression, HPV (oropharynx)
fields.pathology: Most common is SCC (squamous cell carcinoma); lymphoma second in tonsillar fossa; minor glands: adenocarcinoma, adenoid cystic, mucoepidermoid, polymorphous low-grade
fields.clinical: Nonhealing ulcer, bleeding, pain, ill-fitting dentures, vague discomfort, foreign body sensation; advanced: dysarthria, dysphagia, neck mass, referred otalgia; tonsillar: odynophagia, trismus
fields.diagnosis: CBC (complete blood count), CMP (comprehensive metabolic panel), high-risk HPV test, in situ hybridization; CT (computed tomography)/MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) for primary and nodes; chest x-ray and PET (positron emission tomography) for metastases; fiberoptic endoscopy; biopsy; dental evaluation
fields.treatment: Oral cavity: surgical resection; oropharynx: resection + radiotherapy (better function); prevention: tobacco and alcohol cessation
